title: Exam technique: Communication and Networking
content:
### What earns the marks
For switching and protocols, describe earns marks for the mechanism plus its consequence: packets carry addresses and sequence numbers so routers forward independently and the receiver reassembles. For TCP vs UDP, justify earns marks for matching reliability to the use case, not for declaring one better. For security, name earns the control plus what it inspects: packet-filtering checks headers against rules.
### Traps
Error: circuit-switching features credited to packet switching. Correction: dedicated path and guaranteed bandwidth are circuit properties. Error: TCP recommended for live video. Correction: delay hurts more than loss there, so UDP. Error: claiming wireless uses collision detection. Correction: senders cannot listen while sending, so avoidance (RTS/CTS).

title: Binomial Distribution — Study Notes
content:
The Binomial Distribution

When Binomial Applies

X ~ B(n, p) counts successes in n independent trials when:

  • a fixed number n of identical trials,
  • each trial ends in success or failure,
  • constant success probability p,
  • trials are independent.

Check all four before using the model — "justifying a binomial model" is a real exam question.

The Formula

P(X = r) = ⁿCᵣ pʳ(1 − p)ⁿ⁻ʳ for r = 0, 1, ..., n. The ⁿCᵣ counts which r of the n trials were the successes.

Example: X ~ B(5, 0.3). P(X = 2) = ¹⁰C₂? No — ⁵C₂ × 0.3² × 0.7³ = 10 × 0.09 × 0.343 = 0.3087.

Cumulative Probabilities

P(X ≤ 2) = P(0) + P(1) + P(2). "At least" questions convert by the complement: P(X ≥ 2) = 1 − P(X ≤ 1). Keep one extra decimal place in intermediate steps to avoid rounding drift.

Expectation and Variance

  • E(X) = np and Var(X) = np(1 − p)

For X ~ B(20, 0.4): E(X) = 8 and Var(X) = 4.8.

Modelling Decisions

If trials are dependent (drawing without replacement from a small population) binomial is not appropriate. If p changes between trials it is not binomial. When n is large and p small, the binomial is approximately Poisson — but at A2 you usually stay exact.

Exam tips: identify n and p in words before touching the calculator. For P(X ≥ k) always rewrite as 1 − P(X ≤ k − 1). Tables give cumulative values — use them rather than summing by hand.

title: Further Trigonometry — Study Notes
content:
Further Trigonometry

Compound Angles

  • sin(A ± B) = sin A cos B ± cos A sin B
  • cos(A ± B) = cos A cos B ∓ sin A sin B

Example: sin 75° = sin(45° + 30°) = (√2/2)(√3/2) + (√2/2)(1/2) = (√6 + √2)/4.

Double Angles

  • sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A
  • cos 2A = cos²A − sin²A = 2cos²A − 1 = 1 − 2sin²A

Example: express 4 sin x cos x in one term: 2 sin 2x.

The R-Form

a sin x + b cos x = R sin(x + α) with R = √(a² + b²) and tan α = b/a.

Example: 3 sin x + 4 cos x = 5 sin(x + 0.927). This instantly gives the maximum 5 and minimum −5.

Reciprocal Functions

sec θ = 1/cos θ, cosec θ = 1/sin θ, cot θ = 1/tan θ. Key identity: 1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ.

Exam tips: choose the cos 2A form that eliminates the unwanted function; when solving with R-form, divide by R before using inverse trig, and translate intervals carefully.

Exam method: reciprocal functions and identities

The reciprocal functions are sec x = 1/cos x, cosec x = 1/sin x and cot x = 1/tan x. Rewrite them in terms of sine and cosine when a question mixes functions, because this usually shows which identity to use.

The Pythagorean identities are sin² x + cos² x = 1, 1 + tan² x = sec² x and 1 + cot² x = cosec² x. Divide the first identity by cos² x or sin² x to obtain the second or third.

To solve an equation such as sec x = 2, first rewrite it as cos x = 1/2, then find the acute angle and the other solutions in the required range. For cos x = k the solutions in 0 to 2π are α and 2π − α, where α is the acute angle.

To prove an identity, work on the more complicated side only, and keep rewriting until it matches the other side.

Exam cue: Give each solution in the range asked for, using exact values such as π/3 when the angle is standard.

title: Waves & Sound — Study Notes
content:
Waves & Sound

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): general wave properties; reflection/refraction/diffraction; sound.

1. Wave basics

v = fλ. Transverse (oscillation ⊥ travel — light, water, S-waves) vs longitudinal (parallel — sound, P-waves). Amplitude, wavelength, frequency f = 1/T; wavefront diagrams.

2. Ripple tank behaviours

  • Reflection: angle in = angle out; speed/frequency unchanged, direction changes.
  • Refraction: speed change at boundary bends wavefronts (shallow water slows ripples).
  • Diffraction: spreading through gaps ≈ λ wide; around edges.

3. Electromagnetic spectrum (order)

Radio → micro → IR → visible (red 700 nm – violet 400 nm) → UV → X → gamma. All travel at 3 × 10⁸ m/s in vacuum; transverse; uses and dangers (IR heating; UV skin; X/gamma ionising).

4. Sound

  • Longitudinal; needs a medium (bell in vacuum demo). Speed ~340 m/s air, faster in liquids/solids.
  • Range 20 Hz–20 kHz; ultrasound > 20 kHz (sonar, prenatal scans, cleaning).
  • Pitch ↔ frequency; loudness ↔ amplitude.

5. Echo problems

Distance = (v × t)/2 (there and back).

Example: echo after 0.6 s, v = 340 → cliff 102 m away.

Exam tips: in diagrams always label wavelength as crest-to-crest; for refraction, state "changes speed" first, then direction; quote EM uses with the hazard.

Wave equation and sound

The wave equation is v = fλ, where v is the wave speed, f the frequency and λ the wavelength. Sound is a longitudinal wave that needs a medium, so it cannot travel through a vacuum. All electromagnetic waves travel at the speed of light in a vacuum, about 3 × 10⁸ m/s. In reflection the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. For an echo, the sound travels to the reflecting surface and back, so the distance to the surface is half the total distance travelled.

title: Work, Energy and Power — Study Notes
content:
Work, energy and power

Work

  • Work done = force × displacement in the direction of the force, W = Fs cos θ. Unit: joule (J), where 1 J = 1 N m.
  • No work is done by a force that acts perpendicular to the displacement, such as the normal contact force on a body moving along a horizontal surface.

Energy stores and transfers

Gravitational potential energy, kinetic energy, elastic potential energy, chemical energy and thermal energy are energy stores. Work done transfers energy from one store to another.

Conservation of energy

Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred. Where only conservative forces such as gravity act, the total mechanical energy is constant. Where non-conservative forces such as friction or air resistance act, the energy they dissipate appears as thermal energy.

Kinetic and gravitational potential energy

  • Kinetic energy: Ek = ½mv².
  • Gravitational potential energy change near the Earth's surface: ΔEp = mgΔh.

Power and efficiency

  • Power = work done ÷ time = energy transferred ÷ time. Unit: watt (W), where 1 W = 1 J s⁻¹.
  • Efficiency = useful energy output ÷ total energy input × 100%. It is always less than 100%.

Worked example: a 2.0 kg object falls freely from rest through 5.0 m. Its speed at the bottom, from energy conservation: ½mv² = mgh, so v = √(2gh) = √(2 × 9.81 × 5.0) ≈ 9.9 m s⁻¹.

Exam tips: check whether the question says air resistance is negligible before using conservation of energy. Always convert minutes to seconds in power calculations. Give efficiency as a percentage.

Power, efficiency and energy transfer

Power is the rate at which work is done or energy is transferred, P = W/t = Fv for a force moving at constant velocity. Efficiency is the useful energy output divided by the total energy input, and it is always less than 1 because some energy is dissipated, usually as thermal energy from friction. When a body is raised, its gain in gravitational potential energy is mgh, and a kinetic energy change is ½m(v2 - u2). Both can be used to find the work done against resistive forces.

Exam tip: state the percentage efficiency with units, and check that it is below 100 percent.

title: Statistics — Probability — Study Notes
content:
Statistics — Probability

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): probability scale, combined events, tree diagrams, conditional probability, relative frequency.

1. Basics

P(event) = favourable/total; 0 ≤ P ≤ 1; P(not A) = 1 − P(A). Probabilities of a complete set sum to 1 — use to find a missing probability.

2. Combined events

  • Independent: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).
  • Mutually exclusive: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B).
  • With replacement ⇒ independent; without replacement ⇒ denominators shrink.

Example: bag 4 red, 6 blue; two draws without replacement: P(both red) = 4/10 × 3/9 = 2/15.

3. Tree diagrams

Multiply along branches; add between outcome paths. Label end products like 4/10 × 6/9 = 4/15.

4. Conditional probability

P(A|B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B). From tree diagrams it is the "given the first branch happened" re-weighting.

5. Relative frequency (experimental)

Relative frequency = successes ÷ trials. More trials → closer to theoretical probability; compare with expected counts (n × P).

Exam tips: always reduce fractions for final answers; in tree diagrams write the multiplication line before the product — that is where the marks are.

title: Exam technique: Abstract Data Types
content:
### What earns the marks
For ADT choice, the access pattern stated earns the mark: LIFO for stacks, FIFO for queues, keyed jumps for BSTs. For traversals, the visit order written (root-left-right for preorder) earns each mark. For linked structures, pointer relinking described earns the insertion mark without any shifting claim.
### Traps
Error: queues for undo. Correction: undo is LIFO, so stack. Error: inorder claimed as root-first. Correction: preorder is root-first. Error: arrays claimed best for mid-list churn. Correction: shifting costs every insert.
### Worked example
Trace a stack. Push A, push B, push C, then pop, then push D, then pop. After the three pushes the top is C, so the first pop returns C. Pushing D leaves the stack as A, B, D, so the second pop returns D and B is left on top. A stack is last in, first out, so the top item always leaves first.
### Check yourself
State which structure a printer queue uses and why, in one sentence that names the order of service. A print queue serves the first job submitted first, so it is first in, first out.

title: Exam technique: Dynamics
content:
### What earns the marks
For resultant force, subtract opposition before applying F = ma to earn both marks. For collisions, total momentum before equated to total after earns the method mark. For rebounds, the sign change included earns the second mark.
### Traps
Error: friction ignored in acceleration. Correction: use the resultant, not the push alone. Error: rebound treated as stopping. Correction: add the speeds with the sign flip. Error: kinetic energy claimed conserved generally. Correction: momentum always, kinetic only when elastic.
### Worked example
A car of mass 800 kg has a driving force of 2400 N and a resistance of 400 N. The resultant force is 2400 - 400 = 2000 N, so a = F/m = 2000 / 800 = 2.5 m/s^2. Subtract the opposing force before you divide by the mass.
### Check yourself
A 2 kg trolley moving at 3 m/s hits a stationary 1 kg trolley, and they stick together. Total momentum before is 2 x 3 = 6 kg m/s, so the joint speed is 6 / 3 = 2 m/s. Show the momentum equation even when the speed looks obvious.

title: Integration — Study Notes
content:
Integration

Cambridge International AS & A Level Mathematics 9709, Paper 1. Integration reverses differentiation. Questions want a general antiderivative, a specific curve through a point, a definite integral, or an area. Most lost marks come from the constant of integration, the limits, and the sign of a region below the axis.

Start from a question

A curve passes through (1, 1) and has dy/dx = 3√x − 2/x² for x > 0.

  1. Find y in terms of x.
  2. Evaluate the integral of (3√x − 2/x²) from x = 1 to x = 4.
  3. Find the area between the curve y = x² − 4 and the x-axis, from x = 0 to x = 3.

Part 1. Integrate term by term: 3x^(1/2) gives 2x^(3/2), and −2x⁻² gives 2x⁻¹. So y = 2x^(3/2) + 2/x + c. Substituting (1, 1) gives 2 + 2 + c = 1, so c = −3 and y = 2x^(3/2) + 2/x − 3.

Part 2. The antiderivative at 4 is 16 + ½ = 33/2. At 1 it is 4 = 8/2. The definite integral is 33/2 − 8/2 = 25/2. No +c is needed.

Part 3. The curve y = x² − 4 crosses the x-axis at x = 2. Between 0 and 2 it lies below the axis, so that part of the integral is negative. The area is |∫ from 0 to 2| + ∫ from 2 to 3. The first integral is [x³/3 − 4x] from 0 to 2 = −16/3, so its area is 16/3. The second is [x³/3 − 4x] from 2 to 3 = −3 − (−16/3) = 7/3. The total is 23/3. Taking the integral from 0 to 3 directly gives −3, which is the wrong answer for an area.

Indefinite integrals

∫axⁿ dx = a xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + c, for n ≠ −1. Add one to the power, divide by the new power, and write +c. Multiply out brackets and rewrite roots as powers first. Example: ∫(x − 2)(x + 4) dx = ∫(x² + 2x − 8) dx = x³/3 + x² − 8x + c.

Area between two curves

Find where the curves meet, then integrate the upper curve minus the lower curve between those x-values. Example: y = 2x and y = x² meet at x = 0 and x = 2. Between them 2x ≥ x², so the area is ∫ from 0 to 2 of (2x − x²) dx = [x² − x³/3] from 0 to 2 = 4/3.

Trapezium rule

With strips of width h and ordinates y₀, y₁, …, yₙ, the estimate is (h/2)[y₀ + 2(y₁ + … + yₙ₋₁) + yₙ]. Example: ∫ from 0 to 2 of (x² + 1) dx with h = 1. The ordinates are 1, 2 and 5, so the estimate is ½(1 + 4 + 5) = 5. The exact value is 14/3. The curve bends upwards, so the estimate is too large.

Traps that cost marks

  • Integrating a product term by term without expanding the brackets first.
  • Writing +c in a definite integral, or forgetting it in an indefinite one.
  • Subtracting the limits in the wrong order.
  • Quoting a negative answer for an area that lies below the x-axis.

title: Astronomy and Cosmology — Study Notes
content:
Astronomy and Cosmology

Luminosity and Intensity

Luminosity L is total power radiated (W). Intensity at distance d: I = L/(4πd²) — the key to distances.

Standard candles (Cepheid variables, Type Ia supernovae) have known L, so measuring I gives d.

Example: the Sun: I = 1370 W m⁻² at d = 1.5 × 10¹¹ m gives L ≈ 3.9 × 10²⁶ W.

Stellar radii (25.2)

A star radiates as a black body of surface temperature T, so L = 4πR²σT⁴. Rearranged, R = √(L / 4πσT⁴). Luminosity therefore depends on both radius and temperature.

Example: with L = 3.9 × 10²⁶ W and T = 5800 K, R = √(3.9 × 10²⁶ / (4π × 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ × 5800⁴)) ≈ 7.0 × 10⁸ m.

Doubling the temperature at fixed radius multiplies L by 2⁴ = 16. A cool red giant can be far more luminous than the Sun because its radius is very large.

Wien and Stefan–Boltzmann

  • Wien: λ_max T = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K — hotter stars are bluer
  • Stefan: L = σAT⁴, σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸

Hubble's Law

Galaxies recede with v = Hd, H₀ ≈ 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹. Redshift z = Δλ/λ ≈ v/c for small z.

Example: a galaxy at 100 Mpc recedes at v = 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ × 100 × 3.09 × 10²² ≈ 6800 km s⁻¹.

The Big Bang

Evidence: Hubble expansion, cosmic microwave background (2.7 K), hydrogen/helium abundance. Age estimate: t ≈ 1/H₀ ≈ 14 billion years. The fate question: critical density, Ω.

Exam tips: convert Mpc to metres (×3.09 × 10²²) before Hubble arithmetic; distinguish redshift of light from distance ladder methods.

title: Exam technique: Probability
content:
### What earns the marks
For combined events, each branch probability with the changed denominator earns a mark: write 3/5 then 2/4 for no-replacement draws. For expectation, probability times trials stated earns the mark even with arithmetic slips. For conditional probability, restricting the denominator to the given condition earns the method mark: write 12/20 before simplifying. For P(A or B), the overlap subtracted earns the final mark.
### Traps
Error: unchanged denominator after a no-replacement draw. Correction: both numerator and denominator drop. Error: dividing by 50 for a given-glasses probability. Correction: condition first, population second. Error: adding P(A) + P(B) without subtracting the overlap. Correction: both-occurring counted twice. Error: adding single-coin probabilities for two coins. Correction: multiply along branches.

title: Sequences and Series — Study Notes
content:
Sequences and Series

Arithmetic Progressions (AP)

Terms increase by a common difference d.

  • nth term: uₙ = a + (n − 1)d
  • Sum: Sₙ = n/2 [2a + (n − 1)d]

Example: AP 5, 8, 11: the 20th term is 5 + 19 × 3 = 62.

Geometric Progressions (GP)

Terms multiply by a common ratio r.

  • nth term: uₙ = arⁿ⁻¹
  • Sum: Sₙ = a(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r)
  • Sum to infinity (|r| < 1 only): S∞ = a/(1 − r)

Example: a = 8, r = 1/2 gives S∞ = 8/(1/2) = 16.

Binomial Expansion

(1 + x)ⁿ = 1 + nx + n(n − 1)/2! x² + n(n − 1)(n − 2)/3! x³ + …, valid for |x| < 1.

For positive integer n, coefficients come from Pascal's triangle: (1 + 2x)⁴ = 1 + 8x + 24x² + 32x³ + 16x⁴.

Exam tips: identify a, d or r first; for "sum to infinity" questions check |r| < 1 explicitly, and for binomial expansions give terms up to the power asked (usually x² or x³).

title: Exam technique: Sets
content:
### What earns the marks
For Venn problems, the union formula n(A union B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A intersect B) quoted earns the method mark; subtracting the intersection corrects the double count explicitly. For neither, the subtraction from the universal set shown earns the final mark. For notation, the complement symbol with the correct parent set earns precision marks.
### Traps
Error: adding all three Venn counts including the intersection. Correction: the overlap was counted twice, subtract once. Error: element confused with subset (2 vs {2}). Correction: only a set can be a subset. Error: empty set equated with {0}. Correction: {0} has one element; the empty set has none. Error: modal-style single numbers for grouped answers. Correction: classes are intervals.
### Worked example
In a group of 30 students, 18 play football, 12 play hockey and 5 play both. The number who play at least one sport is n(F ∪ H) = 18 + 12 − 5 = 25. The number who play neither is 30 − 25 = 5. Subtracting the overlap avoids counting those 5 students twice.
### Check yourself
Given n(A) = 14, n(B) = 9 and n(A ∩ B) = 4, find n(A ∪ B). It is 14 + 9 − 4 = 19. Then find how many elements are outside both sets if the universal set has 25 elements.

title: Exam technique: Sampling
content:
### What earns the marks
For method choice, random vs stratified vs systematic justified earns the mark. For stratified allocation, the proportion of each stratum applied earns the method mark. For bias discussion, the named source of bias with its effect earns both marks.
### Traps
Error: sample claimed unbiased with no method. Correction: name and justify the method. Error: equal numbers per stratum. Correction: allocate proportionally. Error: population confused with frame. Correction: frame is the list used.
### Worked example
A school has 600 students: 120 in Year 11 and 480 in Year 10. A stratified sample of 50 is needed with proportional allocation. Year 11 gets 120/600 x 50 = 10 students, and Year 10 gets 480/600 x 50 = 40 students. The two numbers add to 50, which confirms the allocation. Random selection then happens inside each group.
### Check yourself
A teacher samples 50 students from the first 50 names on the register. Name the sampling method and the main source of bias. This is a convenience sample, and the bias comes from the register order, which may not represent the whole school.

title: Circular Motion and SHM — Study Notes
content:
Circular Motion and SHM

Circular Motion Recap

Angular speed ω = 2π/T; v = ωr; a = ω²r = v²/r; F = mv²/r toward the centre.

Simple Harmonic Motion

Acceleration is proportional to displacement and opposite: a = −ω²x.

Solutions: x = x₀ sin ωt (start at centre) or x = x₀ cos ωt (start at extreme), with ω = 2πf.

Velocity and acceleration:

  • v_max = ωx₀ at the centre
  • a_max = ω²x₀ at the extremes

Example: a pendulum with x₀ = 0.02 m, f = 0.5 Hz has a_max = (2π × 0.5)² × 0.02 ≈ 0.20 m s⁻².

Energy in SHM

E = ½mω²x₀² total (constant), exchanged between KE (max at centre) and PE (max at extremes).

Damping and Resonance

Damping removes energy: light damping → slow decay; critical → fastest return without oscillation. Resonance: driving at the natural frequency gives maximum amplitude (microwave ovens, swing pushing, bridge disasters).

Exam tips: quote a = −ω²x as the defining condition; time period questions often need only T = 2π/ω.

title: Data Types and File Organisation — Study Notes
content:
Data Types and File Organisation

User-Defined Types

A user-defined type is derived from existing types. An enumerated type lists named values in order: TYPE Months = (Jan, Feb, Mar ...). Internally each value is an integer index starting at 0. Pointer types store a memory address; the dereference operator returns the value at that address, which is how linked structures reference their nodes. Set types store unordered collections of distinct values from an ordinal base type, supporting union, intersection and difference.

Records

A record groups related fields of different types under one identifier, for example a Student record with name : STRING and mark : INTEGER. Arrays of records are the standard structure for storing a table of items in memory.

File Organisation

  • Serial: records in insertion order; searching checks every record. Simple but slow.
  • Sequential: records kept in key order; binary search possible, but insertion needs rewriting.
  • Random (direct): a hashing function converts the key into a storage address, giving near-instant access. A poor hash causes collisions — two keys hashing to the same address — resolved by chaining or overflow areas.

Hashing

A common method is division hashing: Address = Key MOD TableSize. A good hash distributes keys evenly; load factor above roughly 70 percent degrades performance.

Exam tips: state the internal integer representation of enumerated values; define a collision before describing its resolution; compare the three file organisations in terms of search and insert cost.

title: Exam technique: Pressure and Density
content:
### What earns the marks
For solids, p = F/A with substitution earns both marks. For liquids, proportionality with depth stated earns the explanation mark. For hydraulics, pressure equated across pistons earns the method mark.
### Traps
Error: force and pressure interchanged. Correction: pressure divides by area. Error: depth effect inverted. Correction: deeper means greater pressure. Error: atmospheric pressure guessed at 10 Pa. Correction: about 100 kPa at sea level.

title: Electric Fields and Capacitance — Study Notes
content:
Electric Fields and Capacitance

Coulomb's law

The force between two point charges is F = kQ₁Q₂/r², with k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². Like charges repel and unlike charges attract. The force acts along the line joining the charges.

Example: +2.0 μC and −3.0 μC, 0.30 m apart, attract with F = 0.60 N.

Electric field strength

Field strength E is the force per unit positive charge: E = F/Q, in N C⁻¹ (or V m⁻¹). For a point charge E = kQ/r², radially outward for positive charge.

Uniform field: between parallel plates, E = V/d, with the field constant in magnitude and direction. A charge q in it feels F = qE.

Example: plates 4.0 cm apart with p.d. 600 V have E = 1.5 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹.

Electric potential and potential energy

Electric potential V at a point is the work done per unit positive charge in bringing a small charge from infinity to that point: V = kQ/r for a point charge. Potential is a scalar. Field strength is the negative potential gradient, E = −dV/dr, so a steep potential-distance graph means a strong field. The field points from high to low potential.

Capacitance

Capacitance C = Q/V, measured in farads (C V⁻¹). The energy stored is W = ½QV = ½CV² = ½Q²/C. The area under a graph of V against Q equals the stored energy.

Example: a 10 μF capacitor charged to 200 V stores 0.20 J.

Capacitors in series and parallel

  • In parallel the capacitances add: C = C₁ + C₂.
  • In series the reciprocals add: 1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂. The total is smaller than the smallest.

Discharge: through a resistor R, the charge falls exponentially, Q = Q₀e^(−t/RC). The time constant RC is the time for the charge or p.d. to fall to 37% of its initial value.

Exam tips: convert μF and cm to SI units before calculating. Check whether a question asks for field strength (vector) or potential (scalar). Series capacitors share the charge; parallel capacitors share the p.d.

title: Exam technique: Algebra — Equations
content:
### What earns the marks
To earn full marks on this topic, students need to demonstrate the ability to calculate, show that, explain, describe, justify, and state their answers clearly. For 2.5 Equations, students should be able to calculate solutions to linear and quadratic equations, show that their solutions are correct, and explain their methods. When solving simultaneous equations, students should be able to justify their choice of method and state their answers clearly. Working should be shown for all calculations, especially when using the quadratic formula or completing the square.
### Traps
Common mistakes include forgetting to multiply through by the LCD when working with fractions, adding instead of subtracting when eliminating variables in simultaneous equations, and not verifying answers by substituting them back into the original equation. Another trap is not defining the unknown clearly in word problems, leading to incorrect equations.
### Memory hooks
To make this topic easier to remember, students can use the mnemonic 'LCD' to recall the steps for solving linear equations with fractions. They can also use the pattern of 'add, subtract, multiply, divide' to remember the order of operations when solving simultaneous equations. A shortcut for completing the square is to remember that the constant term is always -(b/2)^2 + c. Students can also sanity-check their answers by graphing the related functions or using a calculator to verify their solutions.
### Timing
This topic typically accounts for 10-15% of the total exam time. Students should budget around 20-30 minutes to answer questions on this topic, depending on the difficulty and complexity of the questions. It is essential to read the questions carefully and allocate time accordingly to ensure that all parts of the question are answered.

title: Functions — Study Notes
content:
Functions

A function maps each input in the domain to exactly one output in the range.

Composite Functions

fg(x) means f(g(x)) — apply g first, then f. Order matters.

Example: f(x) = 2x + 1, g(x) = x². Then fg(x) = 2x² + 1 but gf(x) = (2x + 1)².

Inverse Functions

f⁻¹ reverses f: f⁻¹f(x) = x. To find it, swap x and y in y = f(x) and rearrange.

Example: f(x) = 3x − 2 gives f⁻¹(x) = (x + 2)/3.

An inverse exists only if f is one-one. If not, restrict the domain (e.g. f(x) = x² for x ≥ 0 has f⁻¹(x) = √x). Graphically, y = f⁻¹(x) is the reflection of y = f(x) in the line y = x, and the range of f becomes the domain of f⁻¹.

Transformations

NotationEffect on y = f(x)
f(x) + atranslation up by a
f(x + a)translation left by a
a f(x)vertical stretch, factor a
f(ax)horizontal stretch, factor 1/a
−f(x)reflection in the x-axis
f(−x)reflection in the y-axis

Exam tips: state the domain of any inverse; when combining transformations, translations inside the bracket act in the opposite direction to the sign.

title: Exam technique: Mensuration
content:
### What earns the marks
For circles, sectors and arcs, the fraction of 360 stated earns the method mark: write 60/360 before multiplying. For cylinders, cones and spheres, the formula quoted earns a mark on its own, so write Volume = (1/3) pi r squared h even when confident. For compound shapes, split earns marks: compute each part separately, then add or subtract with a clear statement.
### Traps
Error: 2 pi r used for area. Correction: circumference versus area check first. Error: omitting 1/3 for cones and pyramids. Correction: quote the formula every time. Error: using diameter as radius in a semicircle cut-out. Correction: halve the diameter before any pi work. Error: forgetting the square root in a Pythagoras step. Correction: label squared lines as squared.
### Worked example
A cylinder has radius 3 cm and height 10 cm. Its volume is πr²h = π × 9 × 10 = 90π ≈ 282.7 cm³. A sector of angle 60° in a circle of radius 6 cm has arc length (60/360) × 2π × 6 = 2π cm.
### Check yourself
A trapezium has parallel sides 5 cm and 9 cm and a perpendicular height of 4 cm. Find its area. Use ½(a + b)h = ½ × (5 + 9) × 4 = 28 cm². State the units and show the substitution before the final value.

title: Probability — Study Notes
content:
Probability

Basic Rules

For an event A with P(A) = p: 0 ≤ p ≤ 1, and P(A′) = 1 − P(A). For mutually exclusive events, probabilities add: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B). For events that can occur together, subtract the overlap:

  • P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B)

Venn Diagrams

Draw the universe first, then the events. Fill from the intersection outwards: if P(A) = 0.6, P(B) = 0.5 and P(A ∩ B) = 0.25, then only-A = 0.35, only-B = 0.25, neither = 0.15. Every region must sum to 1.

Tree Diagrams

Branch probabilities multiply along a path; outcomes at the end of complete paths add. Draw one branch set per stage of the experiment. For two draws without replacement from a bag of 5 red and 3 blue: P(RR) = (5/8)(4/7) = 20/56.

Conditional Probability

P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B) — the probability of A given that B has occurred. The condition shrinks the sample space.

Example: P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4, P(A ∩ B) = 0.2. Then P(A | B) = 0.2/0.4 = 0.5, so A and B are independent since P(A | B) = P(A).

Independence

A and B are independent exactly when P(A ∩ B) = P(A)·P(B). Do not confuse independent (no influence on probabilities) with mutually exclusive (cannot co-occur). Mutually exclusive events with non-zero probabilities are never independent.

Exam tips: convert every "given that" into a conditional. With trees, label the second-stage branches with conditional probabilities; they are usually different from the first stage when drawing without replacement.

Exam method: combined events

The addition rule gives P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B). For mutually exclusive events the intersection is empty, so P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B). Draw a Venn diagram to place each probability in its region before calculating.

Independent events satisfy P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B). Test independence by checking this equation rather than assuming it, because the question may give the joint probability and ask you to decide.

The conditional probability P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B). Events are independent exactly when P(A | B) = P(A).

Tree diagrams suit sequential events without replacement. Multiply along each branch and add the branches that give the outcome required.

Exam cue: State whether events are independent or mutually exclusive, because the two are different and the formula depends on it.

title: Operating Systems — Study Notes
content:
Operating Systems

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2023–2025): OS roles, memory/process management, hardware–software layer, interrupts, buffers, utility software.

1. What an OS does

Manages memory, processes/files, I/O via drivers, security (users, permissions), and provides the UI (CLI/GUI) between user, applications and hardware.

2. Memory and process management

  • Paging/segmentation move programs in/out; virtual memory extends RAM to disk when RAM is full.
  • Multitasking: scheduler gives each process time slices; context switching saves/restores state.

3. Interrupts and buffers

Interrupts signal events (I/O complete, timer); CPU saves context, services via ISR, resumes. Buffers hold data in transit (printing) so slow devices don't block the CPU; spooling queues jobs.

4. Utility software

Disk formatter, defragmenter (reduces head movement on HDDs; unnecessary for SSD), backup scheduler, compression, antivirus, file compression.

5. UI and drivers

CLI: precise, scriptable, low overhead. GUI: icons/windows, discoverable, more resources. Device drivers translate OS calls to hardware specifics — each device needs its own.

Exam tips: "manage" verbs earn marks: manages memory, manages processes, manages peripherals; explain virtual memory by RAM-full scenario, not definition alone.

Choose a significance level such as 5%, calculate the test statistic and its p-value, then reject H₀ if p < α. title: Energy, Work & Power — Study Notes
content:
Energy, Work & Power

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): stores and transfers, KE/PE, work, energy sources, power, efficiency.

1. Energy stores & transfers

Stores: kinetic, gravitational, elastic, chemical, nuclear, thermal. Transfer mechanisms: mechanically, electrically, heating, waves. Energy is conserved overall; transfers via work done.

2. Formulas

  • KE = ½mv²; PE = mgh.
  • Work W = Fd (force along displacement, joules).
  • Power P = W/t = E/t; P = Fv for constant speed.

Example: 0.5 kg at 4 m/s: KE = 4 J. Lift 2 kg by 3 m: PE = 60 J (g = 10).

3. Energy sources

Renewable: solar, wind, hydro, geothermal, biofuel, tidal — replenished. Non-renewable: fossil fuels, nuclear — finite. Discuss reliability, cost, pollution for "evaluate" questions.

4. Efficiency

Efficiency = useful output ÷ total input (×100%). Sankey diagrams show losses.

Example: motor: 150 J useful from 600 J → 25%.

5. Energy-chain problems

Equating KE loss to PE gain: v = √(2gh) for frictionless drop; braking distance grows with v².

Exam tips: define work as "force × distance moved in the direction of the force"; use g = 10 unless told otherwise; efficiency is a ratio — no units.

title: Numerical Measures of Central Tendency — Study Notes
content:
Central Tendency: Mean, Median and Mode

The Mean

For data x₁, ..., xₙ the mean is

  • x̄ = Σx/n

For a frequency table with midpoints x and frequencies f: x̄ = Σfx/Σf. The mean uses every value, so a single extreme value drags it — that is its main weakness.

The Median

The median is the middle value: position (n + 1)/2 for ordered raw data. With n even, average the two middle values. The median ignores the size of extreme values, so it describes skewed data more honestly. For grouped data, estimate the median by linear interpolation within the median class.

The Mode

The most frequent value. A dataset may have no mode or several. For grouped data the modal class is the one with the highest frequency density (frequency ÷ class width), not the highest frequency.

Effects of Data Changes

Adding a constant a to every value adds a to the mean and median (the mode too) but leaves the spread untouched. Multiplying every value by b multiplies mean and median by b.

Coding

Subtract a constant and divide by a convenient width: y = (x − a)/b. Then x̄ = b·ȳ + a. Coding simplifies arithmetic and always preserves the relationship — the coded mean decodes exactly.

Example: data 2, 4, 4, 10: mean = 5, median = 4, mode = 4. Change 10 to 100: mean = 27.5, median and mode unchanged — the mean chased the outlier.

Exam tips: always state which average you used and why. When asked to compare two distributions, pair a central measure with a spread measure; a mean without a spread is only half an answer.

Exam method: mean, median and mode

For ungrouped data, the mean is the sum of the values divided by the number of values. The median is the middle value of the ordered list, at position (n + 1)/2, and the mode is the value that occurs most often. Always order the data before finding the median.

For grouped data, the mean is Σfx/Σf using the class midpoints. The modal class is the class with the highest frequency, and the median class is the one containing the (n + 1)/2 th value.

Each average suits different data. The mean uses every value, so an outlier pulls it away from the centre, while the median is unaffected by extreme values. Say which average is more representative when the question asks you to comment.

Changing one value changes the mean but may not change the median, which is useful to check a calculation.

Exam cue: When the question gives a mean and asks for a missing value, form the equation Σx = n × mean and solve for the unknown.

title: Continuous Random Variables — Study Notes
content:
Continuous Random Variables

Probability Density Functions

A continuous variable X is described by a density f(x) with f(x) ≥ 0 and ∫f(x)dx = 1 over all x. Probabilities are areas:

  • P(a ≤ X ≤ b) = ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx

Single points have zero probability, so strict or loose inequalities make no difference: P(X < 2) = P(X ≤ 2).

Finding Unknown Constants

Piecewise densities carry an unknown k: impose that the total area is 1 (and continuity at joins where required). One equation, one unknown.

Example: f(x) = kx on 0 ≤ x ≤ 2. Total area: k·(2²/2) = 2k = 1, so k = ½.

Expectation and Variance

  • E(X) = ∫x·f(x) dx
  • E(X²) = ∫x²·f(x) dx
  • Var(X) = E(X²) − (E(X))²

The mean is the balancing point of the area under the density. For symmetric densities the mean sits at the symmetry point — worth spotting before integrating.

The Median and Mode

The median m solves ∫₋∞ᵐ f(x) dx = 0.5 (left half of the area). The mode is the x maximising f(x). For uniform densities the median is the midpoint.

Uniform Distribution

If f(x) = 1/(b − a) on [a, b], every point is equally likely. Then E(X) = (a + b)/2 and Var(X) = (b − a)²/12 — memorise both; they are quick exam marks.

Exam tips: always verify ∫f = 1 before computing anything else. Sketch the density — area intuitions catch algebra slips. Median questions are integration-to-0.5 questions; set them up before calculating.

Exam method: density functions

A probability density function f must satisfy f(x) ≥ 0 for all x and the total area under it must equal 1, so the integral of f over its whole domain is 1. Use this to find an unknown constant before asking for any probability.

For a continuous variable, P(a ≤ X ≤ b) is the integral of f(x) from a to b. The endpoints carry no probability, so strict and non-strict inequalities give the same answer. Outside the given domain f(x) = 0.

The cumulative distribution function F(x) = P(X ≤ x) is the integral of f from the lower end of the domain up to x. The median m satisfies F(m) = 0.5, and the mode is where f is largest.

Expected value E(X) is the integral of x f(x) over the domain, and the variance is E(X²) minus the square of E(X). Write each integral with its limits before evaluating.

Exam cue: Sketch the density over its domain first. A linear density is a triangle or trapezium, and the area of the shape gives the total probability quickly.

title: Further Algebra — Study Notes
content:
Further Algebra

Polynomial Division and the Remainder Theorem

Divide to rewrite p(x) = (x − a)q(x) + r. The remainder when dividing by (x − a) equals p(a).

Example: p(x) = x³ − 2x² + 5. p(2) = 8 − 8 + 5 = 5, so dividing by (x − 2) leaves remainder 5.

If p(a) = 0, then (x − a) is a factor — that is the factor theorem. Divide out fully to reduce a cubic to a quadratic and factorise completely.

The Modulus Function

|x| measures distance from zero: |x| = x for x ≥ 0, −x for x < 0. Its graph is V-shaped.

Solving |2x − 1| = 5: split into 2x − 1 = 5 or 2x − 1 = −5, giving x = 3 or −2.

Inequalities: |2x − 1| < 5 becomes −5 < 2x − 1 < 5, so −2 < x < 3.

Partial Fractions

Reverse of combining fractions — needed before binomial expansion of rational functions.

  • Repeated linear: (4x + 1)/(x + 1)² = A/(x + 1) + B/(x + 1)²
  • Distinct linear: (7x + 4)/(x + 1)(x + 2) = A/(x + 1) + B/(x + 2)

Example: cover the (x + 1) factor with x = −1: B = 3; then compare coefficients for A = 4.

Exam tips: for |ax + b| > c, remember two separate regions; check factor-theorem roots by substitution before long division.

title: Sequences and Series — Study Notes
content:
Sequences and Series

Arithmetic Progressions (AP)

Terms increase by a common difference d.

  • nth term: uₙ = a + (n − 1)d
  • Sum: Sₙ = n/2 [2a + (n − 1)d]

Example: AP 5, 8, 11: the 20th term is 5 + 19 × 3 = 62.

Geometric Progressions (GP)

Terms multiply by a common ratio r.

  • nth term: uₙ = arⁿ⁻¹
  • Sum: Sₙ = a(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r)
  • Sum to infinity (|r| < 1 only): S∞ = a/(1 − r)

Example: a = 8, r = 1/2 gives S∞ = 8/(1/2) = 16.

Binomial Expansion

(1 + x)ⁿ = 1 + nx + n(n − 1)/2! x² + n(n − 1)(n − 2)/3! x³ + …, valid for |x| < 1.

For positive integer n, coefficients come from Pascal's triangle: (1 + 2x)⁴ = 1 + 8x + 24x² + 32x³ + 16x⁴.

Exam tips: identify a, d or r first; for "sum to infinity" questions check |r| < 1 explicitly, and for binomial expansions give terms up to the power asked (usually x² or x³).

Formulae and exam method

Arithmetic progression: the nth term is Tₙ = a + (n − 1)d, where a is the first term and d the common difference. The sum of the first n terms is Sₙ = n/2 [2a + (n − 1)d], or Sₙ = n/2 (a + l) when the last term l is known.

Geometric progression: Tₙ = arⁿ⁻¹, and Sₙ = a(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r) for r ≠ 1. The sum to infinity exists only when |r| < 1, and then S∞ = a/(1 − r).

To find the number of terms, substitute the known sum or term and solve for n. When n sits in an exponent, take logarithms. Check that n is a positive integer.

Sigma notation: Σ from r = 1 to n of (ar + b) is evaluated with the standard sums, but write out the first few terms when the pattern is unclear.

Exam cue: Identify whether the question is AP or GP before choosing a formula, and state the value of r when using the sum to infinity.

Exam method: arithmetic and geometric sums

For an arithmetic sequence with first term a and common difference d, the nth term is a + (n − 1)d and the sum of the first n terms is S_n = n/2 (2a + (n − 1)d). For a geometric sequence with ratio r, the nth term is ar^(n − 1) and S_n = a(1 − r^n)/(1 − r) for r ≠ 1.

The sum to infinity exists only when |r| < 1, and then S∞ = a/(1 − r). If |r| ≥ 1, say so explicitly rather than applying the formula.

Exam cue: Identify whether the sequence is arithmetic or geometric from the common difference or ratio before choosing a formula. Check the number of terms n carefully when you set up the equation.

title: Programming and Algorithms — Study Notes
content:
`# Programming and Algorithms

Design Approaches

  • Top-down (stepwise refinement): decompose into modules — planned structure
  • Object-oriented: classes encapsulating state + behaviour — reusability
  • WAD (write all down): rapid prototyping — evolves during coding

Pseudocode Conventions

DECLARE x : INTEGER
IF x > 10 THEN ... ELSE ... ENDIF
WHILE ... ENDWHILE
FOR i ← 1 TO n ... NEXT i
FUNCTION f(a) RETURNS INTEGER

Searching

  • Linear: check each item, O(n), works unsorted
  • Binary: halve a sorted list each step, O(log n)

Example: 1,000,000 items: binary search needs ≤ 20 comparisons.

Sorting

AlgorithmBestAverageIdea
BubbleO(n)O(n²)swap neighbours
InsertionO(n)O(n²)insert into sorted prefix
MergeO(n log n)O(n log n)divide and merge

Merge sort example: [5,2,9,1] → [5,2][9,1] → [2,5][1,9] → [1,2,5,9].

Recursion

A function calling itself with a base case. Factorial: f(0)=1, f(n)=n·f(n−1). Stack frames handle state.

Exam tips: state the Big-O and justify it; for traces, tabulate variable changes per iteration.

Testing with normal, boundary and erroneous data

Normal test data is typical valid input that the program should accept and process correctly. Boundary (extreme) test data sits at the edges of the valid range, such as the lowest and highest permitted values, because errors often occur there. Erroneous test data is invalid input that the program should reject, such as text entered where a number is required.

A trace table records the value of each variable at each step of an algorithm. Tracing a algorithm by hand with test data shows where it departs from the intended result, and it is a common exam task.

Exam tip: a complete test plan includes all three kinds of data, with the expected output written beside each test value.

title: Further Trigonometry — Study Notes
content:
Further Trigonometry

Compound Angles

  • sin(A ± B) = sin A cos B ± cos A sin B
  • cos(A ± B) = cos A cos B ∓ sin A sin B

Example: sin 75° = sin(45° + 30°) = (√2/2)(√3/2) + (√2/2)(1/2) = (√6 + √2)/4.

Double Angles

  • sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A
  • cos 2A = cos²A − sin²A = 2cos²A − 1 = 1 − 2sin²A

Example: express 4 sin x cos x in one term: 2 sin 2x.

The R-Form

a sin x + b cos x = R sin(x + α) with R = √(a² + b²) and tan α = b/a.

Example: 3 sin x + 4 cos x = 5 sin(x + 0.927). This instantly gives the maximum 5 and minimum −5.

Reciprocal Functions

sec θ = 1/cos θ, cosec θ = 1/sin θ, cot θ = 1/tan θ. Key identity: 1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ.

Exam tips: choose the cos 2A form that eliminates the unwanted function; when solving with R-form, divide by R before using inverse trig, and translate intervals carefully.

title: Coordinate Geometry — Study Notes
content:
Coordinate Geometry

Gradients and Equations of Lines

Gradient m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁). From ax + by + c = 0, the gradient is −a/b.

Point-slope form: y − y₁ = m(x − x₁).

Example: through (4, 3) with m = −1/2: y − 3 = −(x − 4)/2, i.e. y = −x/2 + 5.

Parallel and Perpendicular

  • Parallel lines: equal gradients.
  • Perpendicular lines: m₁m₂ = −1 (gradients are negative reciprocals).

Example: perpendicular to y = 2x + 1 has gradient −1/2.

Midpoint and Distance

Midpoint of (x₁, y₁), (x₂, y₂): ((x₁+x₂)/2, (y₁+y₂)/2).

Distance: √((x₂−x₁)² + (y₂−y₁)²). The line from (0,0) to (3,4) has length 5 — recognise 3-4-5 triangles.

Intersections and Bisectors

Intersections: solve the equations simultaneously. The perpendicular bisector of AB passes through the midpoint of AB with gradient −1/m(AB) — equate distances PA = PB for the locus method.

Exam tips: rationalise gradients as fractions; check perpendicularity by multiplying gradients to get −1.

Key results and exam method

Distance between (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂) is √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²). The midpoint is ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2). The gradient is (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁); a vertical line has no gradient and a horizontal line has gradient 0.

Parallel lines have equal gradients. Perpendicular lines have gradients m₁ and m₂ with m₁m₂ = −1, so a line perpendicular to gradient 3/4 has gradient −4/3. The perpendicular bisector of a chord passes through the midpoint of the chord, is perpendicular to it, and always passes through the centre of the circle.

A circle with centre (a, b) and radius r has equation (x − a)² + (y − b)² = r². Expand and compare with x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 to read the centre (−g, −f) and the radius √(g² + f² − c). To test whether a line meets a circle, substitute the line into the circle equation and examine the discriminant.

Exam cue: Sketch the situation first. Many marks are for stating which point is the midpoint, which gradient is perpendicular, and which radius is used.

Worked example: midpoint, distance and the perpendicular bisector

Let A = (2, 5) and B = (8, −1). The midpoint is ((2 + 8)/2, (5 − 1)/2) = (5, 2). The length AB is √((8 − 2)² + (−1 − 5)²) = √(36 + 36) = 6√2.

The gradient of AB is (−1 − 5)/(8 − 2) = −1. The perpendicular bisector has gradient 1 and passes through (5, 2), so its equation is y − 2 = x − 5, which gives y = x − 3. Check that C = (0, −3) lies on it: 0 − 3 = −3, so it does.

Intersection of two lines

To find where y = 2x + 1 meets y = −x + 7, set the two right-hand sides equal: 2x + 1 = −x + 7, so 3x = 6 and x = 2. Substitute back: y = 2(2) + 1 = 5. The lines meet at (2, 5). Always substitute back into the second equation as a check.

Area of a triangle from coordinates

For the triangle with vertices (1, 1), (5, 1) and (3, 4), the base from (1, 1) to (5, 1) has length 4 and the height is the vertical distance from (3, 4) to that base, which is 3. The area is ½ × 4 × 3 = 6 square units.

When the base is not horizontal, use the shoelace method: list the coordinates in order, multiply diagonally, subtract, and halve the absolute value. It works for any triangle, so it is safer than estimating the height.

Parallel and perpendicular lines in exam questions

  • Parallel lines have equal gradients, so 2y = 4x + 1 and y = 2x − 7 are parallel.
  • Perpendicular gradients multiply to −1, so a line perpendicular to gradient 3/4 has gradient −4/3.
  • If a question asks for a line through a given point perpendicular to a line, find the gradient first, then substitute the point into y = mx + c or y − y₁ = m(x − x₁).

Common errors that lose marks

  • Subtracting the coordinates in different orders for the gradient, for example using (−1 − 5)/(2 − 8), which gives the wrong sign.
  • Stating the distance as the difference of the x-coordinates only, rather than using Pythagoras on both differences.
  • Leaving a midpoint as a fraction when it is a whole number, or giving a line equation in a form that is not what the question asks for.

title: Measures of Variation and Standard Deviation — Study Notes
content:
Measures of Variation

Range and Quartiles

The range is max − min — quick but destroyed by a single outlier. Quartiles split ordered data into quarters: Q₁ at position (n + 1)/4, Q₃ at 3(n + 1)/4 (raw data). The interquartile range, IQR = Q₃ − Q₁, is the spread of the middle 50% and resists outliers. Outliers are commonly flagged as values beyond Q₁ − 1.5·IQR or Q₃ + 1.5·IQR.

Variance and Standard Deviation

For raw data:

  • variance s² = Σ(x − x̄)²/n (the definitional form)
  • equivalently s² = Σx²/n − x̄² (the computational form)
  • standard deviation s = √(variance)

The standard deviation shares the units of the data; the variance does not. For frequency tables use Σf(x − x̄)²/Σf, or Σfx²/Σf − x̄².

Grouped Data

Use class midpoints as x. The result is an estimate — grouping discards within-class detail.

Combining and Scaling Datasets

Multiplying every value by b multiplies s by |b| and the variance by b². Adding a constant changes nothing in the spread. Two merged datasets: compute combined Σx and Σx² from each part, then apply the computational formula.

Example: data 1, 3, 4, 5, 7: mean 4, Σx² = 100, so variance = 100/5 − 16 = 4 and s = 2.

Exam tips: state units for s. When comparing consistency, the dataset with the smaller standard deviation (relative to its mean) is the more consistent. Always give the comparison sentence, not just the two numbers.

Exam method: variance and standard deviation

The variance is the mean of the squared deviations, or equivalently Var(x) = Σx²/n − x̄². The standard deviation is its square root, and it is in the same units as the data. Using the second form is quicker when the mean is already known.

Adding a constant to every value shifts the mean by that constant but leaves the standard deviation unchanged. Multiplying every value by a constant k multiplies the standard deviation by |k| and the variance by k². Use these rules to avoid recalculating from scratch.

For grouped data, use the class midpoints and the frequencies. The variance is Σfx²/Σf − x̄², with x̄ = Σfx/Σf.

The standard deviation is a measure of spread. Compare two data sets by stating which has the larger spread and linking that to the context of the data.

Exam cue: Show the sum of the values and the sum of squares before dividing, because the method marks depend on those totals.

title: Programming Concepts — Study Notes
content:
Programming Concepts

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): variables/constants, data types, selection/iteration, arrays, file handling, subroutines, scope, IDE tools.

1. Basics

Constants vs variables; types: INTEGER, REAL, CHAR, STRING, BOOLEAN, DATE; casting between them. Declaration with meaningful names.

2. Selection and iteration

IF score >= 50 THEN
  grade ← "pass"
ELSE
  grade ← "fail"
ENDIF

CASE OF grade
  "A" : OUTPUT "excellent"
  OTHERWISE : OUTPUT "keep going"
ENDCASE

REPEAT
  INPUT pin
UNTIL pin = storedPin

FOR i ← 1 TO 10 STEP 2 ... NEXT i

WHILE: condition first (may not run); REPEAT: runs at least once.

3. Arrays

Fixed size, indexed (0- or 1-based per spec); 2D arrays: row, column. Bounds errors when index leaves range. Traversal with FOR loops.

4. Files

OPENFILE "data.txt" FOR READ
READFILE "data.txt", line
CLOSEFILE "data.txt"

OPENFILE "log.txt" FOR APPEND
WRITEFILE "log.txt", record

Modes: READ, WRITE (overwrites), APPEND (adds).

5. Subroutines

Procedure (no return) vs function (returns value). Parameters by value (copy) vs reference (original). Local scope inside; global shared — declare deliberately, avoid overuse.

6. IDE tools

Syntax highlighting, autocompletion, breakpoints, single stepping, variable watch — name the tool and its debugging benefit.

Exam tips: use the exam pseudocode style exactly; for 2D arrays, loop rows outer/columns inner; choose WHILE vs REPEAT by "must it run once?"

title: Electricity & Circuits — Study Notes
content:
Electricity & Circuits

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): simple circuits, current, p.d., resistance, series/parallel, electrical safety, practical electricity.

1. Circuit symbols & current

Conventional current: + → − (electron flow opposite). I = Q/t. Ammeter in series; voltmeter in parallel.

2. Current, p.d., e.m.f.

  • Current: rate of charge flow; same everywhere in series.
  • p.d.: energy per coulomb across a component; e.m.f.: electrical energy per coulomb given by the source.

3. Resistance

  • R = V/I. Ohmic conductor: V ∝ I at constant temperature.
  • Series: R = R₁ + R₂ + …; same current; p.d. shares in proportion to R.
  • Parallel: 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂; same p.d.; current splits (inverse-R share).
  • Resistance ∝ length, ∝ 1/area (wires).

4. Components

Fixed/variable resistors, LDR (light ↑ R ↓), thermistor (T ↑ R ↓), diode/LED (one-way), relay, filament lamp (R grows as T rises — V–I curve flattens).

5. Power and energy

P = VI = I²R = V²/R; E = VIt. Fuse rating just above normal current; earth wire, double insulation, circuit breakers (trip quickly, resettable).

Example: 230 V, 2 A heater: P = 460 W; correct fuse 3 A or 5 A.

6. Digital electronics basics (syllabus 4.5 context)

Analogue vs digital; logic gates drive outputs from inputs (see CS link); sensors feed comparator-style circuits.

Exam tips: series: current same; parallel: p.d. same — say which before calculating; always compute total resistance first in mixed circuits.

Ohm's law and resistors

For a conductor at constant temperature, the current is proportional to the potential difference across it, V = IR. In a series circuit, the current is the same at every point and the total resistance is the sum of the individual resistances. In a parallel circuit, the potential difference across each branch is the same and the current divides between the branches.

For two equal resistors in parallel, the combined resistance is half the value of one resistor. A fuse or circuit breaker protects the wiring by breaking the circuit when the current exceeds a safe value.

Exam tip: state whether the circuit is series or parallel before applying a resistance rule.

title: Robotics & AI — Study Notes
content:
Robotics & AI

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): AI characteristics, machine learning basics, robotics/simulation contexts, automated systems.

1. AI characteristics

Systems exhibiting: planning, learning, reasoning, problem-solving, perception, knowledge representation. Narrow (task-specific) vs general AI distinction for discussion answers.

2. Machine learning

Supervised (labelled data — spam filters), unsupervised (clusters — segmentation), reinforcement (rewards — game agents). Training/evaluation loop: train on a set, test on unseen data; overfitting = memorising rather than generalising.

3. Robotics

Components: sensors (input), processors (decision), actuators/motors (output), power. Examples: manufacturing arms, delivery drones, autonomous vehicles (LIDAR + vision). Benefits: precision, 24/7 operation, dangerous jobs; concerns: job displacement, safety, cost.

4. Automated systems & simulation

Sensors → processor → actuators loops (greenhouses, traffic lights, self-checkouts). Simulation models real systems cheaply and safely (flight training, weather, crash tests) — limitations: model quality, missing variables.

5. Ethics of AI

Bias from unrepresentative training data; opacity of decisions; accountability for errors; privacy of training data; effect on employment.

Exam tips: for "describe how AI could be used in X" — tie each AI characteristic to a concrete step in the scenario; for evaluations, give both sides then a justified conclusion.

Sensors, actuators and feedback

A sensor converts a physical quantity, such as light, temperature or pressure, into an electrical signal. An actuator does the opposite: it converts an electrical signal into physical movement, for example by turning a motor. A robot or automated system uses sensors to read its environment, a processor to decide what to do, and actuators to act.

A feedback loop compares the measured value with the required value and adjusts the output to close the gap. A thermostat is a simple example: it switches the heater off when the room reaches the set temperature. Feedback allows a system to correct itself, but a poorly set loop can overshoot or oscillate.

Exam tip: name a sensor and an actuator in any automated system you describe, and explain what the feedback corrects.

title: Data Types and File Organisation — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Data Types and File Organisation

Computer Science — A2. A user-defined type is derived from existing types. An enumerated type lists named values in order: TYPE Months = (Jan, Feb, Mar ...). Internally each value is an integer index starting at 0. Pointer types store a memory address; the dereference operator returns the value at that address, which is how linked structures reference their nodes. Set types store unordered collections of distinct values from an ordinal base type, supporting union, intersection and difference.

Key areas to revise

  • User-Defined Types
  • Records
  • File Organisation
  • Hashing

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example A hash function maps each key to a storage address. If the file has 100 slots and the key is an integer n, the address could be n mod 100. Two keys that give the same address are a collision, and the file must provide a method such as an overflow area to store the second record. ### Check yourself Compare serial and random file organisation. Serial files store records in the order they were added, so searching is slow. Random files use a hash or index to reach a record directly, so retrieval is fast but collisions must be handled.

title: Circular Measure — Study Notes
content:
Circular Measure

Cambridge International AS & A Level Mathematics 9709, Paper 1: radian measure, arc length, and the areas and perimeters of sectors and segments. Every formula here takes its angle in radians — that is the single fact most marks hinge on.

Radians

One radian is the angle at the centre of a circle subtended by an arc whose length equals the radius. The full circumference is 2πr, so a full turn is 2π radians and π radians = 180°.

  • Degrees → radians: multiply by π/180. Example: 150° = 150π/180 = 5π/6 ≈ 2.618 rad.
  • Radians → degrees: multiply by 180/π. Example: 1.5 rad = 1.5 × 180/π ≈ 85.9°.

Learn the common values: 30° = π/6, 45° = π/4, 60° = π/3, 90° = π/2, 180° = π, 360° = 2π. Leave answers in terms of π unless the question asks for a decimal — and when it does, give three significant figures.

Arc Length

s = rθ (θ in radians).

Example: r = 6, θ = π/3 gives s = 6 × π/3 = 2π.

A chord splits the circumference into a minor arc and a major arc, and their lengths add to 2πr. If a question gives the major angle, use θ_major = 2π − θ_minor before substituting.

Sector Area

A = ½r²θ.

Example: r = 5, θ = 1.2 gives A = ½ × 25 × 1.2 = 15.

Minor and major sector areas add to πr². The perimeter of a sector is P = 2r + s = 2r + rθ — the two straight edges count, so an arc length alone is not a perimeter.

Segment Area

A = ½r²(θ − sin θ). For r = 2, θ = π/2: A = 2(π/2 − 1) = π − 2.

The segment is the sector minus the triangle ½r²sin θ — that subtraction is where the formula comes from, and writing it down earns method marks even if the arithmetic slips. Its perimeter is the arc plus the chord, with chord length 2r sin(θ/2).

Putting It Together

Worked example: a sector has radius 8 cm and angle 1.1 rad. Arc length s = 8 × 1.1 = 8.8 cm. Area A = ½ × 64 × 1.1 = 35.2 cm². Perimeter P = 2 × 8 + 8.8 = 24.8 cm.

Rearranging

  • θ = s/r (must be radians)
  • θ = 2A/r²
  • r = s/θ, and r = √(2A/θ) — isolate the squared term first, then take the positive root only, since a radius is a length.

Exam traps: never mix degrees into s = rθ or A = ½r²θ — convert first, and check the calculator is in radian mode. Sketch the sector and mark r and θ before computing. Read whether the question asks for the major or the minor arc, sector, or segment, and confirm area answers carry squared units while arcs and perimeters are plain lengths.

Transformations and Vectors

1. Transformations — full descriptions

  • Reflection: mirror line (x = 0, y = x, y = −x…).
  • Rotation: centre, angle, direction (anticlockwise positive).
  • Translation: column vector.
  • Enlargement: centre + scale factor; negative SF inverts through the centre.

"Enlargement, SF 2, centre (0, 3)" — every word earns a mark.

2. Combined transformations

Apply right-to-left: "reflect in y = x, then rotate 90°" — rotate the reflected image.

3. Vectors

  • Column vector (x; y); magnitude = √(x² + y²).
  • Resultant by component addition; parallel vectors are scalar multiples.
  • Position vectors: AB = OB − OA.

Example: A(1, 2), B(4, 6): AB = (3; 4), |AB| = 5.

4. Vector geometry

Midpoint of AB = ½(a + b). Prove collinearity: show AB = k·BC (shared point). Prove parallelogram: AB = DC. Use route paths: AC = AB + BC.

title: Circular Measure — Study Notes
content:
Circular Measure

Radians

One radian is the angle subtending an arc equal in length to the radius. π radians = 180°.

  • Degrees → radians: multiply by π/180.
  • Radians → degrees: multiply by 180/π.

Common angles: 30° = π/6, 45° = π/4, 60° = π/3, 90° = π/2, 180° = π, 360° = 2π.

Arc Length

s = rθ (θ in radians).

Example: r = 6, θ = π/3 gives s = 2π.

Sector Area

A = ½r²θ.

Example: r = 5, θ = 1.2 gives A = ½ × 25 × 1.2 = 15.

Segment Area

A = ½r²(θ − sin θ). For r = 2, θ = π/2: A = 2(π/2 − 1) = π − 2.

Rearranging

  • θ = s/r (must be radians)

title: Pressure & Density — Study Notes
content:
Pressure & Density

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): pressure & pressure differences in fluids, density review (Extended pressure-depth).

1. Pressure basics

p = F/A (Pa = N/m²). Increase F or decrease A to raise pressure; explain applications (snowshoes, knives, hydraulic press).

2. Liquids

  • Pressure increases with depth: p = ρgh (Extended).
  • Same level, same liquid ⇒ same pressure (hydrostatic paradox).
  • Hydraulic systems transmit pressure — force multiplier: F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂.

3. Atmospheric pressure

~10⁵ Pa at sea level; demonstrated by collapsing can, mercury barometer 760 mmHg; decreases with altitude.

4. Density revisited

ρ = m/V; floating condition; upthrust = weight of displaced fluid (qualitative).

5. Gas pressure (particle model)

Particles collide with walls → force per area. Volume ↓ at same T ⇒ pressure ↑ (more frequent collisions). Temperature ↑ ⇒ faster particles ⇒ more frequent, harder impacts.

Density in more depth

Density is mass per unit volume, ρ = m/V. Its SI unit is kg/m³, and 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³. An object of a given density will float in a fluid only if the fluid has a higher density. To find the density of an irregular solid, measure its mass on a balance and its volume by displacement of water in a measuring cylinder.

Pressure and depth

Pressure is force per unit area, p = F/A, with unit the pascal (Pa = N/m²). In a liquid, the pressure increases with depth, p = hρg, and acts equally in all directions at a given depth. Atmospheric pressure at sea level is about 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa.

Exam tip: convert the area to m² before you calculate pressure, and use the density in kg/m³ in p = hρg.

Worked method for pressure questions

Step 1: write down the force in newtons and the area in m². Step 2: divide, p = F/A. Step 3: if the question is about a liquid, use p = hρg with h in metres, ρ in kg/m³ and g = 10 N/kg, and remember that the pressure is the same at equal depths in the same liquid. Atmospheric pressure is added to the liquid pressure when a question asks for total pressure at depth.

title: Algebra — Graphs — Study Notes
content:
Algebra — Graphs

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): straight lines (gradient, intercept), key curves (quadratic, cubic, reciprocal, exponential), tangents, kinematic reading.

1. Straight lines

  • Gradient m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁).
  • y = mx + c; parallel ⇒ equal m; perpendicular ⇒ m₁m₂ = −1.

Example: through (2, −1) parallel to y = 3x + 1: y + 1 = 3(x − 2) ⇒ y = 3x − 7.

2. Drawing curves

Table of values, plot, smooth curve. Parabola symmetry axis x = −b/2a. Recognise reciprocal y = 1/x (two branches) and exponential y = aˣ (through (0,1)).

3. Interpreting

  • Roots = x-intercepts; y-intercept from x = 0.
  • Turning points of quadratics by completing the square.

4. Tangents and rates

Gradient of tangent at a point = instantaneous rate: draw a large triangle, rise/run. Area under a speed–time graph = distance (trapezium estimate).

5. Graphical solutions

Simultaneous: intersection points. Quadratic = line: intersections give roots. Read off carefully to the accuracy allowed.

Exam tips: quote gradients as fractions where exact; when estimating a tangent gradient, use a triangle spanning at least 4 grid squares.

Plotting and reading straight-line graphs

A table of values is set up from the equation, points are plotted and joined with a ruler. For y = mx + c, m is the gradient and c the y-intercept. The gradient is the change in y divided by the change in x, measured on a large triangle drawn on the line, not between two points read from a table.

Quadratic and cubic curves

Curves are drawn freehand as smooth curves through plotted points. Turning points, roots (where the curve cuts the x-axis) and the y-intercept are read directly from the graph. A quadratic has one turning point; a cubic can have up to two.

Using graphs to solve equations

To solve f(x) = k, draw the line y = k and read the x-coordinates where it meets the curve. Intersections of two graphs give simultaneous solutions. Always state the solutions to the accuracy the question asks for.

Worked example: gradient and equation of a line

A line passes through (1, 3) and (4, −3). The gradient is (−3 − 3)/(4 − 1) = −6/3 = −2. Substituting into y = mx + c with the point (1, 3) gives 3 = −2 + c, so c = 5 and the equation is y = −2x + 5.

A parallel line has the same gradient, so a line through (0, 1) parallel to this one is y = −2x + 1. A perpendicular line has gradient 1/2.

Turning points of a quadratic

For y = x² − 6x + 5, complete the square: y = (x − 3)² − 4. The minimum turning point is (3, −4), and the curve crosses the x-axis where (x − 3)² = 4, that is at x = 1 and x = 5. Sketch the curve through these points and label the turning point.

Gradient of a curve at a point

Between two points on a curve, the average rate of change is the gradient of the chord. To estimate the gradient at a point, draw a tangent by eye and find its gradient from two clearly read points on the tangent, using a large triangle. The answer will only be as accurate as your tangent.

Reading a graph in context

A distance–time graph has gradient equal to speed, so a horizontal section means the object is stationary. A speed–time graph has gradient equal to acceleration, and the area under it equals the distance travelled. Always state the units of the gradient, for example m/s or m/s².

  • Plot points carefully and join curves with a smooth line, not straight segments.
  • When a question asks you to use a graph to solve an equation, draw the line y = (the right-hand side) and read off the x-values where the curve crosses it.

title: Exam technique: Nuclear Physics (A2)
content:
### What earns the marks
For energy, mass defect times c squared with units earns both marks. For decay, ln2 over half-life quoted earns the method mark; activity as lambda N earns the second. For radii, the cube-root rule applied to ratios earns the mark.

Error: half-life used as the decay constant. Correction: divide ln2 by it. Error: fission named for the Sun. Correction: fusion powers stars. Error: radius scaled linearly with A. Correction: cube root of nucleon number.
### Worked example
A nucleus has a half-life of 8 days. The decay constant is lambda = ln 2 / 8, which is about 0.087 per day. If the sample holds N = 2.0 x 10^10 nuclei, the activity is A = lambda N, about 1.7 x 10^9 decays per day. Quote the unit with the answer, because the mark depends on it.

A nucleus with A = 64 has radius r = 1.2 x 64^(1/3) = 4.8 fm. State why doubling A does not double the radius. The radius grows with the cube root of A, so doubling A multiplies r by 2^(1/3), about 1.26.

title: Exam technique: Networking & Communication
content:
### What earns the marks
For full marks on 2.1, explain why serial transmission is reliable over distance and describe the benefits of packet switching, including robustness and shared lines. For 2.2, state the purpose of checksums and explain how they detect errors. For 2.3, describe the process of encryption and justify its importance in secure data transmission. For 3.4, describe the functions of network hardware components, including routers, switches, and gateways.
### Traps
Error: confusing MAC and IP addresses. Correction: MAC addresses are burned-in and used for layer 2 communication, while IP addresses are assigned and used for layer 3 communication. Error: assuming parallel transmission is always faster. Correction: parallel transmission is faster over short distances, but serial transmission is more reliable over long distances. Error: thinking that HTTPS is a protocol. Correction: HTTPS is HTTP over TLS, a secure protocol for data transmission.
### Memory hooks
Use the mnemonic 'Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away' to remember the layers of the TCP/IP stack: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Application. To compare MAC and IP addresses, use a table to highlight their differences. To remember the functions of network hardware components, associate each component with its function, such as routers 'routing' traffic between networks.
### Timing
This topic typically accounts for 20-30% of the paper, and students should budget around 30-40 minutes to answer questions on networking and communication. Make sure to allocate time to read the questions carefully and plan your answers before starting to write.

title: Communication and Networking — Study Notes
content:
`# Communication and Networking

Transmission

  • Serial: one bit at a time — cheaper, reliable over distance
  • Parallel: multiple bits simultaneously — fast but suffers skew and crosstalk over long runs
  • Direction: simplex (one way), half-duplex (alternating), full-duplex (both ways)

Packets and Protocols

Data splits into packets with header (addresses, sequence) and trailer (checksum). A protocol is an agreed rule set — without one, devices cannot interpret signals.

  • TCP/IP stack: application → transport → network → link
  • HTTP/HTTPS: web transfer; HTTPS encrypts with TLS
  • FTP: file transfer; SMTP/POP3/IMAP: email

Network Types

  • LAN: small site, privately owned; WAN: large geographic scale (the internet)
  • Topologies: bus, star, mesh (star is most common — central switch)

Hardware

Routers join networks by IP; switches forward frames by MAC within a LAN; gateways translate protocols.

Client-Server vs Peer-to-Peer

Client-server: central services, easy administration, single point of failure. P2P: every node shares files directly — cheap, hard to manage (torrents, blockchain).

Exam tips: explain packet switching with header/trailer details; justify protocol choice per application (email vs streaming).

title: Quantum Physics — Study Notes
content:
Quantum Physics

Photons

E = hf = hc/λ, h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.

Example: green light 550 nm: E ≈ 3.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J ≈ 2.3 eV.

The Photoelectric Effect

Light above a threshold frequency ejects electrons instantly; intensity alone does nothing below f₀.

  • Einstein: hf = φ + KE_max (φ = work function)
  • KE_max = eV_s (stopping potential)

Example: sodium φ = 2.3 eV needs λ < 540 nm; 400 nm light gives KE_max = 3.1 − 2.3 = 0.8 eV.

Wave–Particle Duality

de Broglie: λ = h/p = h/(mv). Electrons diffract like waves — electron microscopes exploit short electron wavelengths.

Example: an electron at 10⁶ m s⁻¹: λ ≈ 0.7 nm.

Energy Levels and Line Spectra

Atoms absorb/emit photons matching level gaps: hf = E₁ − E₂. Emission lines are bright; absorption dark.

Example: the Hα line: 3 → 2 transition, 656 nm.

Exam tips: one photon interacts with one electron — that is why intensity cannot release electrons below threshold; convert eV ↔ J with 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹.

title: Trigonometry — Right-Angled Triangles — Study Notes
content:
Trigonometry — Right-Angled Triangles

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): SOH CAH TOA, exact values, angles of elevation/depression.

1. The ratios

Label sides first (opposite, adjacent, hypotenuse) with respect to the marked angle, then choose:

  • sin θ = opp/hyp; cos θ = adj/hyp; tan θ = opp/adj.

Example: hyp 10, angle 35°, find opposite: x = 10 sin 35° = 5.74 (3 s.f.).

2. Finding angles

Use inverse keys: θ = sin⁻¹(opp/hyp). tan θ = 3/4 ⇒ θ = 36.9° (1 d.p.).

3. Exact values (Extended)

θsincostan

45°√2/2√2/21

4. Elevation and depression

Elevation: angle up from horizontal; depression: down. Both measured from the horizontal line at the observer.

Example: tower 20 m, elevation to top 42° → horizontal distance = 20/tan 42° = 22.2 m.

5. Pythagoras combinations

Find a missing side with Pythagoras before applying a ratio when two sides are known instead of an angle.

Exam tips: never round mid-calculation (keep full calculator accuracy); 3 s.f. for lengths, 1 d.p. for angles unless stated.

SOH CAH TOA

In a right-angled triangle with angle θ: sin θ = opposite ÷ hypotenuse, cos θ = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse and tan θ = opposite ÷ adjacent. Label the sides relative to the angle you are using before choosing the ratio. Use Pythagoras to find a missing side first if needed.

Finding angles

To find an angle, use the inverse function, sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹ or tan⁻¹, on the calculator. Set the calculator to degree mode and check that the answer is sensible for the triangle drawn.

Bearings and angles of elevation

An angle of elevation is measured up from the horizontal, and an angle of depression down from it. Draw a clear right-angled triangle from the description to choose the correct ratio. Round the answer to the accuracy in the question, and keep full accuracy in intermediate steps.

title: Exam technique: Poisson Distribution
content:
### What earns the marks
For lambda scaling, the rate times the interval stated earns the first mark. For probabilities, e^-lambda lambda^x / x! with values earns the method mark. For approximations, the condition named (n large, p small, lambda = np) earns credit.
### Traps
Error: unscaled lambda over a new interval. Correction: scale first. Error: binomial coefficients inside Poisson work. Correction: Poisson formula only. Error: mean and variance treated as different. Correction: both equal lambda.
### Worked example
Calls arrive at a rate of 3 per minute, so over 2 minutes λ = 6. The probability of exactly 2 calls is P(X = 2) = e⁻⁶ × 6² / 2! = 18e⁻⁶ ≈ 0.0446. The mean and the variance both equal λ, so the mean number in 2 minutes is 6.
### Check yourself
Explain why the rate must be scaled before you use the formula. The rate is given per minute, but the interval is 2 minutes, so λ must be the rate multiplied by the interval, giving 6 and not 3.

title: Nuclear Physics — Study Notes
content:
Nuclear Physics

The nucleus

The nucleus holds protons and neutrons, collectively nucleons. Nuclide notation ᴬZX gives Z protons and A nucleons, so N = A − Z neutrons. Isotopes share Z and differ in N. Nuclear densities are about 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³, so nearly all the mass of an atom sits in a tiny volume.

Mass defect and binding energy (23.1)

The mass of a nucleus is less than the sum of the masses of its separate nucleons. This difference is the mass defect Δm. Energy equivalent to Δm, given by E = Δmc², is the binding energy: the energy released when the nucleus is assembled from separate nucleons, and the energy needed to separate it. In nuclear work, 1 u = 931 MeV.

Example: a mass defect of 0.0300 u corresponds to E = 0.0300 × 931 ≈ 27.9 MeV.

The binding energy per nucleon peaks near iron-56, the most tightly bound nucleus. Energy is released when the nucleons move toward this peak, by fission of heavy nuclei or by fusion of light ones.

Radioactive decay (23.2)

Decay is random and spontaneous. The effect of each type on the nucleus and its penetration are:

TypeWhat changesStopped by
alphaZ − 2, A − 4paper
beta-minusZ + 1, A unchangeda few mm of aluminium
gammano change to Z or Athick lead

The activity A = λN is the rate of decay, in becquerel (Bq). The decay constant λ and the half-life t½ are related by λ = ln 2 / t½. The number of nuclei left after time t is N = N₀e^(−λt).

Example: a sample with t½ = 10 days has 1/8 of its original activity after 30 days, since three half-lives have passed.

Example: with t½ = 5.0 h = 1.8 × 10⁴ s, λ = 0.693 / 1.8 × 10⁴ ≈ 3.9 × 10⁻⁵ s⁻¹.

Fission and fusion

Heavy nuclei split (fission) into lighter nuclei of greater binding energy per nucleon, which releases energy in reactors. Light nuclei merge (fusion), which releases energy in stars.

Exam tips: balance Z and A on both sides of every decay equation. Convert the half-life to seconds before finding λ. Use A = λN, not guesswork with halves, when the number of nuclei is needed.
