title: Web Technologies and Security — Study Notes
content:
Web Technologies and Security

The Three Layers

  • HTML gives structure and content: elements, attributes, forms for user input.
  • CSS gives presentation: selectors, properties, responsive layout.
  • JavaScript gives client-side behaviour: validation before submission, DOM updates without reload.

Server-side scripting (PHP) runs on the server: reads form fields ($_POST), queries the database, outputs HTML. The client never sees PHP source.

SQL Injection

An attack where crafted input changes the meaning of a query. If a login query concatenates the username directly, entering X OR 1=1 can match every row. Defences: parameterised queries (prepared statements) that separate code from data, validation, and least-privilege database accounts.

Encryption

  • Symmetric: one shared key (AES). Fast, but key distribution is the weak point.
  • Asymmetric: public/private key pair (RSA). Anyone encrypts with the public key; only the holder decrypts with the private key. Slower, so used to exchange a symmetric session key.
  • SSL/TLS combines both: certificates verify the server, asymmetric key exchange establishes a symmetric session key, then traffic is encrypted. HTTPS = HTTP over TLS on port 443.

Hashing vs Encryption

Hashing (e.g. SHA-256) is one-way: passwords should be stored hashed with a unique salt, never encrypted reversibly.

Exam tips: explain why parameterised queries stop injection; describe the TLS handshake in three steps; distinguish hashing from encryption with password storage as the example.

title: Magnetic Fields and Electromagnetism — Study Notes
content:
Magnetic Fields and Electromagnetism

Force on a Current

F = BIL sin θ (Fleming's left hand: field-index, current-first-finger, force-thumb).

Example: 0.5 m wire carrying 3 A at 90° to a 0.2 T field: F = 0.3 N.

Force on a Moving Charge

F = BQv sin θ, always perpendicular to v → circular paths: r = mv/(BQ) (basis of cyclotrons and mass spectrometers).

Example: an electron (m = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg) at 2 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ in 0.5 mT: r ≈ 2.3 cm.

Fields from Currents

  • Long straight wire: B = μ₀I/(2πr), circling by the right-hand grip rule
  • Solenoid: B = μ₀nI inside

Electromagnetic Induction

Faraday: induced EMF = rate of flux cutting = N dΦ/dt. Lenz: induced effects oppose the change (negative sign).

Example: a coil of 100 turns, flux changing 2 mWb in 50 ms induces EMF = 100 × 0.002/0.05 = 4 V.

Flux Φ = BA (B ⊥ A). Generators rotate coils in fields; transformers link two coils by a shared changing flux with V₁/V₂ = N₁/N₂.

Exam tips: use left hand for motors (force on current), right hand for generators (induced current); state Lenz's law in explain questions.

title: Trigonometry — Sine and Cosine Rules — Study Notes
content:
Trigonometry — Sine and Cosine Rules

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): area formula, sine rule, cosine rule, multi-step bearing and 3-D problems (Extended).

1. Area of a triangle

A = ½ab sin C (C = included angle between sides a and b).

Example: a = 8, b = 5, C = 48° → A = ½ × 8 × 5 × sin 48° = 14.8.

2. Sine rule

a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C. Use when a matching angle–side pair is known.

Example: A = 40°, a = 7, B = 65°: b = 7 sin 65°/sin 40° = 9.98.

Ambiguous case: two triangles possible when finding an angle — check the obtuse option (180° − θ).

3. Cosine rule

a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A. Use with two sides + included angle, or all three sides (then cos A = (b² + c² − a²)/(2bc)).

Example: b = 7, c = 5, A = 52°: a² = 74 − 70 cos 52° = 30.9 → a = 5.56.

4. Bearing problems

Draw both north lines, transfer angles via parallel lines, then pick sine/cosine rule.

Example: QP = 60 km bearing 070° from Q; QR = 45 km bearing 150°. ∠PQR = 80° → PR² = 60² + 45² − 2·60·45 cos 80° → PR = 68.4 km.

5. 3-D trigonometry

Identify the plane containing the required angle; use 3-D Pythagoras d² = x² + y² + z² for space diagonals; angle between a line and a plane uses the projection onto the plane.

Exam tips: state which rule you are using and why; sketch a separate 2-D triangle for 3-D questions; answers to 3 s.f. / bearings as three digits.

The sine rule

For any triangle with sides a, b, c opposite angles A, B, C: a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C. Use it when you know a pair of opposite side and angle (for example, two angles and a side, or a side and its opposite angle with another side). Find the missing angle using the angle sum of 180° first.

The cosine rule

a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A, and cos A = (b² + c² − a²) ÷ 2bc. Use it when you know two sides and the included angle, or all three sides. Careful with negative cosines: an obtuse angle gives a negative cos value.

Area of a triangle

Area = ½ab sin C, using two sides and the included angle. This avoids finding the perpendicular height.

Primary keys, foreign keys and relationships

A primary key uniquely identifies each record in a table, so no two records can share its value. A foreign key is a field in one table that holds the primary key of a related table, and it creates a relationship between the tables. Relationships can be one-to-one, one-to-many or many-to-many. A many-to-many relationship is usually split into two one-to-many relationships through a linking table.

Foreign keys stop a record being added that points to a row which does not exist, which keeps the data consistent. Storing each fact once in the correct table also reduces redundancy, so an update is made in one place only.

Exam tip: when designing a table, name the primary key and say which field links it to another table.

title: Hypothesis Testing — Study Notes
content:
Hypothesis Testing

The Framework

The null hypothesis H₀ is the default claim (no change, p = p₀). The alternative H₁ is what a suspicious observation suggests (p > p₀, p < p₀, or p ≠ p₀). The significance level α is the probability of rejecting a true H₀ — the false-alarm rate, usually 5% or 1%.

Test for a Binomial Proportion

With X ~ B(n, p₀) under H₀, compute the probability of results at least as extreme as the observed count in the direction of H₁.

Example: H₀: p = 0.3 against H₁: p > 0.3, observed 10 successes in n = 20. Compute P(X ≥ 10) under B(20, 0.3). If that tail probability is below α, reject H₀.

One-Tailed vs Two-Tailed

One-tailed tests take the whole α in one direction. Two-tailed tests split α across both tails: compare against α/2 on each side, or equivalently check whether the observation falls in the extreme 2.5% (for α = 5%). Choose the tails from the wording of H₁, not from the data.

Critical Regions

The critical region is the set of values of the test statistic that would lead to rejection. Its boundary is the critical value. For B(20, 0.3) at the 5% level with H₁: p > 0.3, find the smallest k with P(X ≥ k) < 0.05 — that k opens the critical region.

Conclusions in Context

Never just say "reject H₀". Conclude in the language of the problem: "there is sufficient evidence at the 5% level that the proportion has increased". State the significance level, the direction, and the real-world quantity.

Exam tips: define H₀ and H₁ with symbols AND words. Verify which tail the observation sits in before computing. If the observed value lies in the critical region, evidence supports H₁; otherwise there is insufficient evidence — never "prove H₀ true".

title: Networking & Communication — Study Notes
content:
Networking & Communication

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): transmission modes, serial/parallel, packet switching, protocols, LAN/WAN, hardware, security layers.

1. Transmission basics

  • Serial: one bit at a time — reliable over distance, cheaper cable.
  • Parallel: several bits at once — faster over short runs; skew/crosstalk limit distance.
  • Simplex / half-duplex / full-duplex direction; bandwidth (bits/s) vs bit rate.

2. Packets

Header (sender/receiver addresses, sequence number) + payload + trailer (checksum). Packet switching: routes vary, packets reassembled at destination; checksum failure → re-request. Benefits: robustness, shared lines; delays/reassembly overhead.

3. Protocols

TCP/IP stack layers (application, transport, network, link). HTTP/HTTPS (TLS encryption), FTP (with login + commands), email: SMTP send, POP3/IMAP retrieve. Bluetooth/Wi-Fi for WPAN/WLAN.

4. Network types & hardware

LAN (site) vs WAN (internet). Router (joins networks, IP), switch (MAC frames within LAN), gateway (protocol translation), NIC, WAP. MAC address (burned-in, layer 2) vs IP address (assigned, layer 3).

5. Security in transmission

Encryption scrambles plaintext → ciphertext (key needed); HTTPS = HTTP over TLS; firewall packet filtering by port/IP; authentication (user+pass, 2FA); access levels.

Exam tips: explain why skew limits parallel over distance; compare MAC vs IP in a table; protocol questions want "rules for communication", not acronyms alone.

title: Differentiation II — Study Notes
content:
Differentiation II

Product and Quotient Rules

  • (uv)′ = u′v + uv′
  • (u/v)′ = (u′v − uv′)/v²

Example: y = x² e^x gives dy/dx = 2x e^x + x² e^x = e^x(2x + x²).

Standard Derivatives

  • sin x → cos x; cos x → −sin x; tan x → sec²x
  • e^x → e^x; ln x → 1/x

Chain Rule Everywhere

d/dx [ln(3x)] = 3/(3x) = 1/x; d/dx [e^(2x)] = 2e^(2x); d/dx [sin²x] = 2 sin x cos x.

Implicit Differentiation

Differentiate both sides w.r.t. x, treating y as a function of x (terms in y pick up dy/dx).

Example: x² + y² = 25 → 2x + 2y(dy/dx) = 0 → dy/dx = −x/y.

Parametric Curves

For x = f(t), y = g(t): dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt).

Example: x = t², y = t³ gives dy/dx = 3t²/2t = 3t/2.

Exam tips: quote the rule you use; for tangent/normal on parametric curves, find t at the point first, and simplify implicit answers using the original equation.

title: Exam technique: Computational Thinking
content:
### What earns the marks
For recursion, the base case quoted plus the shrinking argument earns both marks. For dry runs, each call tracked with its print earns method credit. For strategy choice, the signature named (splitting for divide-and-conquer, retreating for backtracking) earns the mark with a fitting example.
### Traps

title: Databases — Study Notes
content:
`# Databases

Relational Basics

Tables (relations) of records with fields. Keys:

  • Primary key: unique identifier
  • Foreign key: references another table's PK — creates relationships
  • Candidate/secondary keys: other unique identifiers

Normalisation

  • 1NF: atomic values, no repeating groups
  • 2NF: 1NF + no partial dependency on a composite key
  • 3NF: 2NF + no transitive dependencies (non-key → non-key)

Example: (StudentID, Course, CourseFee) has CourseFee depending on Course, not StudentID — move course data to its own table (3NF).

SQL

SELECT name, grade FROM students
  WHERE grade >= 'A' ORDER BY name;
INSERT INTO students VALUES (...);
UPDATE students SET grade = 'B' WHERE id = 5;
DELETE FROM students WHERE id = 5;

Joins combine tables: FROM students s JOIN enrolments e ON s.id = e.sid.

Transactions

ACID: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (rules hold), Isolation (no interference), Durability (committed = permanent). Record locking prevents conflicting simultaneous edits.

Exam tips: justify each normal form step with the dependency removed; write SQL with correct WHERE clauses to avoid accidental full-table updates.

Primary keys, foreign keys and redundancy

A primary key is a field, or combination of fields, that uniquely identifies each record in a table. A foreign key is a field in one table that holds the primary key of a record in another table. Foreign keys link the tables together and let the database check referential integrity, so that an order cannot refer to a customer who does not exist.

Storing data in one place rather than repeating it in several tables reduces data redundancy. Less redundancy saves storage, and it reduces the chance that an update is made in one copy but not the others. Normalisation is the process of organising tables to remove this repetition.

Exam tip: when asked about a foreign key, say which table it sits in and which primary key it refers to.

title: Exam technique: Sine and Cosine Rules
content:
### What earns the marks
For the sine rule, the matched pairs written (b / sin 65 = 7 / sin 40) earn the method mark. For the cosine rule, the full substitution with cos evaluated earns the mark: write a squared = 25 + 64 - 2 x 5 x 8 x 0.5. For the largest angle, identifying the longest side first earns credit. For area, half a b sin C quoted earns the mark on its own.
### Traps
Error: sides paired with wrong angles in the sine rule. Correction: each side faces its angle. Error: 49 given as side a. Correction: root the cosine-rule result. Error: calculator-only acute angle for an obtuse ambiguous case. Correction: subtract from 180 by hand. Error: half a b without sine for a non-right triangle. Correction: area needs the sine factor unless the angle is 90 degrees.
### Worked example
Two sides are 7 cm and 9 cm, with an included angle of 40 degrees. The cosine rule gives x^2 = 7^2 + 9^2 - 2 x 7 x 9 x cos 40 = 130 - 126 x 0.766 = 33.5, so x is about 5.79 cm. Use the cosine rule when you have two sides and the angle between them.
### Check yourself
A right-angled triangle has legs 6 and 8. Compute the area as one half of 6 x 8 x sin 90 degrees, and the hypotenuse with the cosine rule. The area is 24, and the hypotenuse is sqrt(36 + 64) = 10, because cos 90 degrees is zero.

title: Earth & Space — Study Notes
content:
Earth & Space

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): Earth & Solar System; stars & the Universe (Extended).

1. Earth, Moon, Sun

Earth rotates 24 h (day/night), orbits 365¼ d (year + leap). Moon orbits Earth ~27.3 d; phases from viewing angle; lunar/solar eclipses when aligned. Seasons from axial tilt (23.5°), not distance.

2. Solar system

Planets (Mercury → Neptune), dwarf planets (Pluto), moons, asteroids, comets (eccentric orbits, tails away from Sun), natural satellites. Gravity keeps orbits; orbital speed & radius relate to the central mass.

3. Orbital motion

Orbital speed v = 2πr/T. T grows with r (Kepler trend). Comets speed up near the Sun (ellipse, Sun at focus).

4. Stars (Extended)

Star formation: nebula → protostar (gravity, KE→thermal) → main sequence (hydrogen fusion: H→He, radiation pressure balances gravity) → red giant → white dwarf (Sun-mass) or supergiant → supernova → neutron star/black hole (massive stars). Elements heavier than iron form in supernovae.

5. Universe (Extended)

The Sun is one star in the Milky Way; the Milky Way is one of billions of galaxies. Redshift: receding galaxies show stretched wavelengths → the Universe is expanding → Big Bang model; CMB is the afterglow. Hubble: farther ⇒ faster recession.

6. Scales

light-year = distance light travels in a year (9.5 × 10¹⁵ m); astronomical unit = Earth–Sun distance (1.5 × 10¹¹ m).

Orbits and the Solar System in more depth

The planets orbit the Sun because the Sun's gravity provides the centripetal force that keeps them on their paths. A moon is a natural satellite that orbits a planet, and an artificial satellite is launched by people. The Earth rotates once on its axis in one day, and it orbits the Sun once in one year. The phases of the Moon are caused by the changing proportion of its sunlit side that we see as it orbits the Earth.

Exam tip: state the object that provides the gravitational force when you describe why an orbit is stable.

title: Differentiation — Study Notes
content:
Differentiation

Cambridge International AS & A Level Mathematics 9709, Paper 1. Differentiation answers one question: how fast is y changing with x at a given point? Most questions either ask for the gradient function or use it at a particular point.

The power rule

If y = axⁿ then dy/dx = naxⁿ⁻¹, for any rational n. A constant term differentiates to zero. Write roots and reciprocals as powers before you start: √x = x^(1/2) and 1/x² = x⁻².

Example: y = 4√x − 6/x². Rewriting gives y = 4x^(1/2) − 6x⁻², so dy/dx = 2x^(−1/2) + 12x⁻³ = 2/√x + 12/x³.

Expand before you differentiate

Differentiation works term by term, so multiply out any brackets first. Differentiating each factor separately does not give the derivative of the product.

Example: y = (x + 2)(x − 5) = x² − 3x − 10, so dy/dx = 2x − 3.

Tangents and normals

Substitute the x-value into the original curve to get y, and into dy/dx to get the gradient. The tangent uses that gradient; the normal uses the negative reciprocal. Write both in the form y − y₁ = m(x − x₁) and then simplify.

Example: y = x³ − 2x at x = −1. Then y = 1 and dy/dx = 3x² − 2 = 1. The tangent is y = x + 2. The normal has gradient −1 and is y = −x, which also passes through (−1, 1).

Stationary points and their nature

Stationary points are where dy/dx = 0. Solve that equation for x, then use the second derivative: d²y/dx² > 0 gives a minimum and d²y/dx² < 0 gives a maximum. If the second derivative is zero at the point, check the sign of dy/dx on either side of it instead.

Example: y = x³ − 6x² + 9x. Then dy/dx = 3(x − 1)(x − 3), so the stationary points are at x = 1 and x = 3. Since d²y/dx² = 6x − 12, the point at x = 1 is a maximum at (1, 4), and the point at x = 3 is a minimum at (3, 0).

Increasing and decreasing

The curve increases where dy/dx > 0 and decreases where dy/dx < 0. For the example above, dy/dx is positive for x < 1 and for x > 3, and negative between them.

Common errors

  • Differentiating a product factor by factor instead of expanding it first.
  • Forgetting to subtract one from the power, or differentiating a constant to anything other than zero.
  • Giving the tangent without its point, or using the tangent's gradient for the normal.
  • Giving only the x-value of a stationary point instead of its coordinates (x, y).

title: Algebra — Equations — Study Notes
content:
Algebra — Equations

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): linear equations, simultaneous equations, quadratic formula, completing the square, forming equations from words.

1. Linear equations

3(x − 2) = x + 4 → 3x − 6 = x + 4 → 2x = 10 → x = 5. With fractions, multiply through by the LCD first.

2. Forming equations

Translate shapes/situations: "rectangle length 3 cm more than width, perimeter 34" → 2w + 2(w + 3) = 34 → w = 7.

3. Simultaneous equations

  • Elimination: 2x + y = 7 and x − y = 2 → add → 3x = 9 → x = 3, y = 1.
  • Substitution for linear–quadratic: substitute y = 2x into x² + y² = 20 → 5x² = 20 → x = ±2.

4. Quadratics by formula

x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a.

Example: 2x² − 4x − 3 = 0 → x = (4 ± √(16 + 24))/4 = 2.58 or −0.58 (2 d.p.).

5. Completing the square

x² + bx + c = (x + b/2)² − (b/2)² + c. x² − 6x + 5 = (x − 3)² − 4 → minimum at (3, −4). Use for turning points and for solving when factorising fails.

Exam tips: substitute answers back to verify; in word problems define the unknown clearly ("let w = width in cm"); give quadratic solutions to the accuracy demanded.

Solving linear equations step by step

Collect the unknown on one side and the numbers on the other, undoing operations in the reverse order to BODMAS. Whatever you do to one side you must do to the other. When brackets are present, expand first, then collect like terms. Fractions are cleared by multiplying every term by the lowest common denominator.

Simultaneous equations

Two linear equations in x and y can be solved by elimination (make the coefficient of one unknown equal and opposite, then add or subtract) or by substitution (rearrange one equation for one unknown and put it into the other). Check the answer in both original equations. Examiners award method marks for a correct, clearly shown elimination even when arithmetic slips later.

Rearranging formulae

Treat the subject letter as the unknown and apply inverse operations. Where the subject appears twice, gather every term containing it, factorise, then divide. Square roots or squares are undone with a square and a root, applied to both sides.

Worked example: equations with fractions

Solve 3(x − 2)/4 = x + 1. Multiply both sides by 4 to clear the denominator: 3(x − 2) = 4(x + 1), so 3x − 6 = 4x + 4, which gives −10 = x. Check by substitution: left side 3(−12)/4 = −9 and right side −10 + 1 = −9. Both agree, so x = −10.

Examiners award the method mark for clearing the fraction correctly, so write the line where every term is multiplied by the denominator before you expand.

Unknowns on both sides

Solve 5x + 3 = 2x − 9. Subtract 2x from both sides to get 3x + 3 = −9, then subtract 3 to get 3x = −12, so x = −4. Keeping the unknowns on the side where the coefficient stays positive avoids negative-sign slips.

Quadratics and the discriminant

For ax² + bx + c = 0, the discriminant b² − 4ac decides how many real roots there are. If it is positive there are two distinct real roots, if it is zero there is one repeated root, and if it is negative there are no real roots.

Example: 2x² + 3x − 5 = 0 has discriminant 9 + 40 = 49. The formula gives x = (−3 ± 7)/4, so x = 1 or x = −2.5. Check x = 1: 2 + 3 − 5 = 0.

Common errors that lose marks

  • Dividing both sides of an equation by a variable, which can lose a solution (for example x² = 4x has solutions 0 and 4).
  • Applying the quadratic formula with the wrong sign on b, for example writing −3 when b = +3 in the formula.
  • Stopping at a rearranged formula without isolating the subject, or leaving a square root unsimplified when the question asks for an exact answer.

title: Exam technique: Simplifying and Expanding
content:
### What earns the marks
For expansion, calculate earns a mark for every correct pair of products shown before collecting terms. For factorisation, the HCF stated earns the first mark and the fully divided bracket earns the second: partial factorisation scores at most half. For algebraic fractions, factorise first earns the method mark even when cancellation follows.
### Traps
Error: (x + 5)(x - 2) = x squared + 10. Correction: four products, then collect. Error: 3(2x squared - 3x) called fully factorised. Correction: extract x as well. Error: cancelling terms instead of factors in a fraction. Correction: factorise numerator and denominator first.
### Worked example
Expand (2x − 3)(x + 4). The four products are 2x², 8x, −3x and −12. Collecting terms gives 2x² + 5x − 12. For factorisation, 6x² − 9x has HCF 3x, so 6x² − 9x = 3x(2x − 3). Check by expanding the answer back to the original expression.
### Check yourself
Factorise 4x² − 9 completely. It is a difference of two squares: (2x − 3)(2x + 3). Mark schemes often award the first mark for recognising the form, so state it before writing the brackets.

title: Electricity: D.C. Circuits — Study Notes
content:
Electricity: D.C. circuits

Current and charge

  • Current I = charge Q ÷ time t, so Q = It. Unit: ampere (A), where 1 A = 1 C s⁻¹.
  • Electron drift velocity is very small, but the electric field propagates through the circuit almost at the speed of light.

Potential difference and power

  • Potential difference V = energy transferred ÷ charge. Unit: volt (V), where 1 V = 1 J C⁻¹.
  • Power P = VI = I²R = V²/R. Unit: watt (W).

Resistance and resistivity

R = V/I (Ohm's law for an ohmic conductor, at constant temperature). For a wire of length L and cross-sectional area A, R = ρL/A, where ρ is the resistivity in Ω m. Resistance rises with length and falls with area.

Practical circuits

An ammeter is connected in series with the component it measures. A voltmeter is connected in parallel with the component. An ideal ammeter has zero resistance; an ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance.

Kirchhoff's laws

  • First law: at a junction, the total current entering equals the total current leaving (conservation of charge).
  • Second law: around any closed loop, the sum of the emfs equals the sum of the potential differences (conservation of energy).

Potential dividers

For two resistors R1 and R2 in series across a supply V, the potential difference across R2 is V × R2/(R1 + R2).

Worked example: a 100 Ω and a 300 Ω resistor are in series across 12 V. The current is 12/400 = 0.030 A, and the voltage across the 300 Ω resistor is 0.030 × 300 = 9.0 V.

Exam tips: draw the meter in the correct place, in series or in parallel. Apply Kirchhoff's first law to currents and the second law to loops, with consistent signs. Check that units are converted (e.g. mm² to m²) before using ρL/A.

title: Exam technique: Sequences and Series
content:
### What earns the marks

An arithmetic progression has a = 5 and d = 3. The 20th term is a + 19d = 5 + 57 = 62. The sum of the first 20 terms is S₂₀ = (20/2)(2a + 19d) = 10 × 67 = 670. A geometric progression with terms 2, 6, 18 has r = 3, so S₅ = 2(3⁵ − 1)/(3 − 1) = 242. The sum to infinity exists only when |r| < 1, so for r = 1/2 with a = 8 the sum is 8 / (1 − 1/2) = 16.

title: Processor Fundamentals — Study Notes
content:
`# Processor Fundamentals

The FDE Cycle

  • Fetch: PC → MAR; read memory → MDR; instruction → CIR; PC increments
  • Decode: control unit interprets the opcode
  • Execute: ALU/registers act; results stored; PC may be overwritten (jumps)

Registers

RegisterRole
PCaddress of next instruction
MARaddress being accessed
MDRdata in transit
CIRcurrent instruction
ACCaccumulator results

Buses

  • Address bus: one-way, CPU → memory (width sets addressable space)
  • Data bus: two-way, carries instructions/data
  • Control bus: timing and command signals

Interrupts

Signals that pause the current program (I/O complete, timer, errors). The CPU saves context, runs the ISR, then resumes — enabling multitasking.

Assembly and Addressing

Immediate (#5), direct (address holds value), indirect (address points to address), indexed (base + offset — arrays), relative (PC + offset — jumps).

Example: LDD 100 loads from 100 (direct); LDI 100 loads from the address stored at 100 (indirect).

Exam tips: trace register contents step by step in trace tables; explain the stored program concept — instructions as data in memory.

The fetch-decode-execute cycle and registers

The program counter (PC) holds the address of the next instruction. During fetch, that address is copied to the memory address register (MAR), the instruction is read into the memory data register (MDR) and then into the current instruction register (CIR), and the PC is incremented. During decode the control unit works out what the instruction means, and during execute the ALU or another part of the CPU carries it out.

The accumulator is a register that holds the results of arithmetic and logic operations. Registers are very fast storage inside the CPU, and the CPU uses them so that it does not have to wait for main memory on every step.

Exam tip: learn the purpose of each register in one sentence. Examiners often ask which register holds the address, and which holds the instruction.

title: Exam technique: Dynamics
content:
### What earns the marks

### Traps
Error: friction ignored in acceleration. Correction: use the resultant, not the push alone. Error: rebound treated as stopping. Correction: add the speeds with the sign flip. Error: kinetic energy claimed conserved generally. Correction: momentum always, kinetic only when elastic.
### Worked example
A car of mass 800 kg has a driving force of 2400 N and a resistance of 400 N. The resultant force is 2400 - 400 = 2000 N, so a = F/m = 2000 / 800 = 2.5 m/s^2. Subtract the opposing force before you divide by the mass.
### Check yourself

Mensuration — Bearings and Loci

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): compass bearings, scale drawings, constructions (perpendicular/angle bisectors), loci regions.

1. Bearings

  • Measured clockwise from north; three figures: 065°, 128°, 300°.
  • Back bearing = front bearing ± 180°.
  • Draw a north line at both points; north lines are parallel, giving Z-angles.

Example: B is on bearing 070° from A → A is on bearing 250° from B.

2. Scale drawings

1 cm : 500 m style scales; measure, convert, and quote distances/bearings from your drawing to the accuracy allowed.

3. Constructions

  • Perpendicular bisector of a segment: equal arcs from both ends, join the crossings.
  • Angle bisector: equal arcs from the vertex arms.
  • 60° and 90° constructions with compasses; leave all arcs visible.

4. Loci

Fixed distance from a point = circle; from a line = parallel lines with rounded ends; equidistant from two points = perpendicular bisector; from two lines = angle bisector.

Example: a goat tied by a 5 m rope to a corner of a 4 m × 6 m shed: the reachable region is ¾ circle radius 5 m + two ¼ circles radius 1 m where the rope wraps.

Exam tips: state "clockwise from north" in bearing definitions; shade/label locus regions clearly; use a ruler for construction lines too.

title: Pressure & Density — Study Notes
content:
Pressure & Density

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): pressure & pressure differences in fluids, density review (Extended pressure-depth).

1. Pressure basics

p = F/A (Pa = N/m²). Increase F or decrease A to raise pressure; explain applications (snowshoes, knives, hydraulic press).

2. Liquids

  • Pressure increases with depth: p = ρgh (Extended).
  • Same level, same liquid ⇒ same pressure (hydrostatic paradox).
  • Hydraulic systems transmit pressure — force multiplier: F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂.

3. Atmospheric pressure

~10⁵ Pa at sea level; demonstrated by collapsing can, mercury barometer 760 mmHg; decreases with altitude.

4. Density revisited

ρ = m/V; floating condition; upthrust = weight of displaced fluid (qualitative).

5. Gas pressure (particle model)

Particles collide with walls → force per area. Volume ↓ at same T ⇒ pressure ↑ (more frequent collisions). Temperature ↑ ⇒ faster particles ⇒ more frequent, harder impacts.

Density in more depth

Density is mass per unit volume, ρ = m/V. Its SI unit is kg/m³, and 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³. An object of a given density will float in a fluid only if the fluid has a higher density. To find the density of an irregular solid, measure its mass on a balance and its volume by displacement of water in a measuring cylinder.

Pressure and depth

Pressure is force per unit area, p = F/A, with unit the pascal (Pa = N/m²). In a liquid, the pressure increases with depth, p = hρg, and acts equally in all directions at a given depth. Atmospheric pressure at sea level is about 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa.

Exam tip: convert the area to m² before you calculate pressure, and use the density in kg/m³ in p = hρg.

title: Binomial Distribution — Study Notes
content:
The Binomial Distribution

When Binomial Applies

X ~ B(n, p) counts successes in n independent trials when:

  • a fixed number n of identical trials,
  • each trial ends in success or failure,
  • constant success probability p,
  • trials are independent.

Check all four before using the model — "justifying a binomial model" is a real exam question.

The Formula

P(X = r) = ⁿCᵣ pʳ(1 − p)ⁿ⁻ʳ for r = 0, 1, ..., n. The ⁿCᵣ counts which r of the n trials were the successes.

Example: X ~ B(5, 0.3). P(X = 2) = ¹⁰C₂? No — ⁵C₂ × 0.3² × 0.7³ = 10 × 0.09 × 0.343 = 0.3087.

Cumulative Probabilities

P(X ≤ 2) = P(0) + P(1) + P(2). "At least" questions convert by the complement: P(X ≥ 2) = 1 − P(X ≤ 1). Keep one extra decimal place in intermediate steps to avoid rounding drift.

Expectation and Variance

  • E(X) = np and Var(X) = np(1 − p)

For X ~ B(20, 0.4): E(X) = 8 and Var(X) = 4.8.

Modelling Decisions

If trials are dependent (drawing without replacement from a small population) binomial is not appropriate. If p changes between trials it is not binomial. When n is large and p small, the binomial is approximately Poisson — but at A2 you usually stay exact.

Exam tips: identify n and p in words before touching the calculator. For P(X ≥ k) always rewrite as 1 − P(X ≤ k − 1). Tables give cumulative values — use them rather than summing by hand.

Exam method: binomial probabilities

If X ~ B(n, p) then X counts successes in n independent trials, each with probability p. P(X = r) = nCr p^r (1 - p)^(n - r) for r = 0, 1, ..., n. The mean is np and the variance is np(1 - p).

Check the conditions first: a fixed number of trials, two outcomes, a constant p and independent trials. If any condition fails, the binomial model does not apply.

title: Nuclear Physics — Study Notes
content:
Nuclear Physics

The nucleus

The nucleus holds protons and neutrons, collectively nucleons. Nuclide notation ᴬZX gives Z protons and A nucleons, so N = A − Z neutrons. Isotopes share Z and differ in N. Nuclear densities are about 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³, so nearly all the mass of an atom sits in a tiny volume.

Mass defect and binding energy (23.1)

The mass of a nucleus is less than the sum of the masses of its separate nucleons. This difference is the mass defect Δm. Energy equivalent to Δm, given by E = Δmc², is the binding energy: the energy released when the nucleus is assembled from separate nucleons, and the energy needed to separate it. In nuclear work, 1 u = 931 MeV.

Example: a mass defect of 0.0300 u corresponds to E = 0.0300 × 931 ≈ 27.9 MeV.

The binding energy per nucleon peaks near iron-56, the most tightly bound nucleus. Energy is released when the nucleons move toward this peak, by fission of heavy nuclei or by fusion of light ones.

Radioactive decay (23.2)

Decay is random and spontaneous. The effect of each type on the nucleus and its penetration are:

TypeWhat changesStopped by
alphaZ − 2, A − 4paper
beta-minusZ + 1, A unchangeda few mm of aluminium
gammano change to Z or Athick lead

The activity A = λN is the rate of decay, in becquerel (Bq). The decay constant λ and the half-life t½ are related by λ = ln 2 / t½. The number of nuclei left after time t is N = N₀e^(−λt).

Example: a sample with t½ = 10 days has 1/8 of its original activity after 30 days, since three half-lives have passed.

Example: with t½ = 5.0 h = 1.8 × 10⁴ s, λ = 0.693 / 1.8 × 10⁴ ≈ 3.9 × 10⁻⁵ s⁻¹.

Fission and fusion

Heavy nuclei split (fission) into lighter nuclei of greater binding energy per nucleon, which releases energy in reactors. Light nuclei merge (fusion), which releases energy in stars.

Exam tips: balance Z and A on both sides of every decay equation. Convert the half-life to seconds before finding λ. Use A = λN, not guesswork with halves, when the number of nuclei is needed.

Nuclear decay and half-life

Alpha particles are helium nuclei with two protons and two neutrons, and they are strongly ionising but have low penetration. Beta-minus emission happens when a neutron changes into a proton and an electron is emitted. Gamma radiation is electromagnetic, carries no charge and no mass, and has high penetration. Background radiation must be subtracted from measured count rates before a half-life is calculated.

title: Ethics, Security & Impact — Study Notes
content:
Ethics, Security & Impact

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2023–2025): ethics & professional codes, security threats, malware, online safety, environmental/employment impact.

1. Ethics and codes

ACM/IEEE-CS/BCS codes: public interest, competence, integrity, privacy. Applying: identify the principle → apply to scenario → stakeholders affected → consequences.

2. Threats

  • Malware: virus (attaches, replicates via host), worm (self-spreads), trojan (disguised), spyware, ransomware.
  • Social: phishing (fake emails/sites), pharming (DNS/hosts redirect), shoulder surfing, brute force.
  • Technical: interception (packet sniffing), SQL injection (malicious input into queries), DoS (flooding services).

3. Defences

Antivirus/antispyware (scan, quarantine), firewalls (port/IP filtering), 2FA + biometrics, strong passwords + managers, encryption (HTTPS, VPN), access levels, patches/updates, user training.

4. Online behaviour

Digital footprint, cyberbullying, fake news, privacy settings, verification of sources.

5. Wider impact

Employment: automation displaces roles but creates IT jobs. Environment: e-waste, energy use vs paperless efficiency. Monitoring: workplace tracking, CCTV — balance with privacy laws (GDPR-style).

Exam tips: name the threat precisely (pharming ≠ phishing), then the matched defence; ethics answers need principle + application, not opinion.

title: Thermal Physics — Study Notes
content:
Thermal Physics

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): kinetic particle model; thermal expansion; specific heat capacity; melting/boiling; conduction, convection, radiation.

1. Kinetic model

Solid: fixed positions, vibrate — fixed shape/volume. Liquid: move around, touching — fixed volume, flows. Gas: far apart, fast random motion — fills container. Brownian motion evidences random molecular motion.

2. Gas pressure and temperature

Pressure from wall collisions. Heating at fixed volume → faster particles → more frequent, harder collisions → higher pressure.

3. Thermal expansion

Heating → particles vibrate more → solids expand slightly (gases expand most). Applications: bimetallic strip (fire alarm/thermostat), gaps in bridges/rails; the liquid-in-glass thermometer.

4. Specific heat capacity

c = ΔE/(mΔθ). Heating: ΔE = mcΔθ.

Example: 2 kg water (c = 4200), 20→80 °C: ΔE = 2×4200×60 = 504 kJ.

High c of water → coolant; temperature rise measured with known heater power P in time t: c = Pt/(mΔθ).

5. State changes

Melting/boiling at fixed temperature despite heating (energy breaks bonds, not temperature). Condensation/ freezing release energy. Impurities raise melting point of mixtures/lower freezing; boiling needs nucleation.

6. Transfer: conduction, convection, radiation

  • Conduction: mainly metals (delocalised electrons + lattice vibration); non-metals poor; insulators trap air.
  • Convection: hot fluid expands, density falls, rises; denser cool fluid sinks — currents.
  • Radiation: infrared EM waves; no medium; matte black best absorber/emitter, shiny silver worst.

Applications: vacuum flask, house insulation, car radiators, solar heating panels.

title: Differentiation — Study Notes
content:
Differentiation

Basic Rules

  • d/dx (xⁿ) = n xⁿ⁻¹
  • d/dx (k) = 0, d/dx (kx) = k

Example: y = 5x² − 3x gives dy/dx = 10x − 3.

Chain Rule

dy/dx = dy/du × du/dx.

Example: y = (3x − 1)⁵: dy/dx = 5(3x − 1)⁴ × 3 = 15(3x − 1)⁴.

Tangents and Normals

The tangent gradient at a point is dy/dx there; the normal gradient is −1/(dy/dx).

Example: y = x² at (2, 4): tangent y = 4x − 4; normal has gradient −1/4.

Stationary Points

Set dy/dx = 0, then classify with the second derivative:

  • d²y/dx² > 0 → minimum
  • d²y/dx² < 0 → maximum
  • d²y/dx² = 0 → test either side

Example: y = x³ − 3x: dy/dx = 3x² − 3 = 0 at x = ±1; d²y/dx² = 6x, so a maximum at x = −1 and a minimum at x = 1.

Rates of Change

dy/dx is a rate: if V = 4/3 πr³, then dV/dr = 4πr² links volume change to radius change.

Exam tips: always restart gradients from the derivative at the exact point, and answer rate questions with units.

Rules and exam method

For y = axⁿ, dy/dx = naxⁿ⁻¹. Differentiate each term of a polynomial separately; a constant term differentiates to zero. Rewrite roots and reciprocals as powers first: √x = x^(1/2) and 1/x² = x⁻².

Product rule: d/dx(uv) = u dv/dx + v du/dx. Quotient rule: d/dx(u/v) = (v du/dx − u dv/dx)/v². Chain rule: dy/dx = dy/du × du/dx. For (ax + b)ⁿ the result is na(ax + b)ⁿ⁻¹.

Stationary points occur where dy/dx = 0. Classify them by the sign of dy/dx either side of the point, or with d²y/dx²: positive gives a minimum, negative a maximum, and zero means use the sign change. The gradient at a point gives the tangent; the normal has the negative reciprocal gradient.

Exam cue: Give the tangent or normal as y − y₁ = m(x − x₁), or simplified to y = mx + c, as the question asks. Check it by substituting the point back into the line.

title: Exam technique: Indices and Standard Form
content:
### What earns the marks

For standard form, the coefficient between 1 and 10 with the power justified by the point shift earns both marks. For surds, the split into square factor times prime remainder earns the method mark, and rationalising must finish simplified.

Error: unsimplified 6 root 3 / 3 accepted as final. Correction: always cancel to 2 root 3. Error: non-standard-form coefficients (45 x 10 to the -5). Correction: one non-zero digit, then fix the power.

title: Sampling and Estimation — Study Notes
content:
Sampling and Estimation

Populations, Samples, Statistics

A parameter describes the population (μ, σ²); a statistic describes the sample (x̄, s²). A statistic is unbiased if its expectation equals the population parameter: E(x̄) = μ always holds for the sample mean.

Unbiased Variance

The estimator with divisor (n − 1) is the unbiased sample variance:

  • s² = Σ(x − x̄)²/(n − 1)

Why n − 1: deviations are measured from x̄ rather than μ, slightly underestimating spread; the smaller divisor corrects it. At A2, state which estimator you are using — the unbiased one is the default.

Distribution of the Sample Mean

For a sample of size n from a population with mean μ and variance σ²:

  • E(x̄) = μ and Var(x̄) = σ²/n

Averaging shrinks spread — bigger samples give steadier estimates.

Central Limit Theorem

Whatever the population shape, for large n (rule of thumb n ≥ 30) the sample mean is approximately normal: x̄ ~ N(μ, σ²/n). This is why the normal appears constantly in inference.

Example: population mean 50, s.d. 12, n = 36. Then x̄ ~ N(50, 4) and P(x̄ > 51) = P(Z > 0.5) = 0.3085.

Using x̄ to Estimate

Given sample data, estimate μ by x̄ and σ² by the unbiased s². When the population is normal, x̄ is exactly normal for any n — the CLT is only needed for non-normal populations.

Exam tips: distinguish σ²/σ (population) from s²/s (sample) in notation. Standard error means √(σ²/n) — smaller with larger n. Quote probabilities for x̄ with the variance divided by n; forgetting that division is the classic error.

title: Trigonometry — Sine and Cosine Rules — Study Notes
content:
Trigonometry — Sine and Cosine Rules

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): area formula, sine rule, cosine rule, multi-step bearing and 3-D problems (Extended).

1. Area of a triangle

A = ½ab sin C (C = included angle between sides a and b).

Example: a = 8, b = 5, C = 48° → A = ½ × 8 × 5 × sin 48° = 14.8.

2. Sine rule

a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C. Use when a matching angle–side pair is known.

Example: A = 40°, a = 7, B = 65°: b = 7 sin 65°/sin 40° = 9.98.

Ambiguous case: two triangles possible when finding an angle — check the obtuse option (180° − θ).

3. Cosine rule

a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A. Use with two sides + included angle, or all three sides (then cos A = (b² + c² − a²)/(2bc)).

Example: b = 7, c = 5, A = 52°: a² = 74 − 70 cos 52° = 30.9 → a = 5.56.

4. Bearing problems

Draw both north lines, transfer angles via parallel lines, then pick sine/cosine rule.

Example: QP = 60 km bearing 070° from Q; QR = 45 km bearing 150°. ∠PQR = 80° → PR² = 60² + 45² − 2·60·45 cos 80° → PR = 68.4 km.

5. 3-D trigonometry

Identify the plane containing the required angle; use 3-D Pythagoras d² = x² + y² + z² for space diagonals; angle between a line and a plane uses the projection onto the plane.

Exam tips: state which rule you are using and why; sketch a separate 2-D triangle for 3-D questions; answers to 3 s.f. / bearings as three digits.

title: Number — Arithmetic and Place Value — Study Notes
content:
Number — Arithmetic and Place Value

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): 1.1 integers & place value; 1.2 fractions/decimals/percentages context; 1.3 powers & roots; HCF/LCM.

1. Types of number

  • Integers: … −2, −1, 0, 1, 2 … Primes: exactly two factors; 2 is the only even prime; 1 is not prime.
  • HCF = product of common prime factors (lowest powers); LCM = all prime factors (highest powers).

Example: 60 = 2²×3×5 and 84 = 2²×3×7 ⇒ HCF = 2²×3 = 12; LCM = 2²×3×5×7 = 420.

2. Place value

In 47 382 the digit 7 has value 7000. Rounding to significant figures: keep n digits, round using the next digit (≥5 up).

Estimation: round inputs to 1 s.f. first — 39.2 × 5.98 ≈ 40 × 6 = 240.

3. Order of operations

BIDMAS. 3 + 4 × 2² = 3 + 16 = 19. Insert brackets yourself when translating words: "3 added to the product of 4 and 2²" = 3 + (4 × 2²).

4. Negative numbers and calculators

Bracket negatives when substituting. Know the ×10ˣ, x², √, ˣ√ and fraction keys; give answers to 3 s.f. unless told otherwise.

5. Bounds (Extended)

Measured to nearest u: UB = +u/2, LB = −u/2. Division p/q: max = UBp ÷ LBq.

Example: 45 cm (nearest cm) in 6 s (nearest s): max speed = 45.5 ÷ 5.5 = 8.27 m/s (3 s.f.).

Exam tips: show prime-factor trees for HCF/LCM; always state rounding units (3 s.f., 1 d.p.); bounds answers quote both limits.

Five values are 2, 4, 4, 6 and 9. The mean is 25 / 5 = 5. The squared deviations are 9, 1, 1, 1 and 16, which sum to 28. The variance is 28 / 5 = 5.6, and the standard deviation is the square root, about 2.37. Show the squared deviations line on the paper, since the method mark depends on it.

If each value in the list is increased by 10, state what happens to the mean and to the standard deviation. The mean rises by 10, while the standard deviation is unchanged, because adding a constant does not change the spread.

title: Motion in a Circle and Gravity — Study Notes
content:
Motion in a circle and gravity

Circular motion

  • A body moving in a circle at constant speed has a centripetal acceleration of v²/r, directed towards the centre.
  • The centripetal force is F = mv²/r = mω²r, and it is provided by a real force such as tension, friction or gravity. It does no work on the body, because it is always perpendicular to the velocity.

Gravitational field

The gravitational field strength at a point is the force per unit mass placed at that point: g = F/m. Unit: N kg⁻¹. Field lines point towards the mass that creates the field.

Newton's law of gravitation

F = GMm/r², where r is measured from the centre of each point mass. Doubling the separation reduces the force to one quarter.

Gravitational field of a point mass

g = GM/r². Outside a uniform sphere, its field is the same as that of a point mass at its centre.

Gravitational potential

Gravitational potential at a point is the work done per unit mass in bringing a small mass from infinity to that point. It is always negative, is zero at infinity, and becomes more negative closer to the mass: V = −GM/r. Gravitational potential energy of a mass m is Ep = mV.

Worked example: a 2.0 kg object moves in a circle of radius 0.50 m at 3.0 m s⁻¹. The centripetal force is F = mv²/r = (2.0 × 3.0²) ÷ 0.50 = 36 N.

Exam tips: use r as the distance from the centre, not the surface. State that gravitational potential is negative and rises to zero at infinity. Field strength and potential are different quantities: do not mix their units.

Gravitational potential and escape velocity

Gravitational potential at a point is the work done per unit mass in moving a small mass from infinity to that point, so φ = -GM/r. Potential is negative because work must be done against gravity to remove a mass to infinity. The change in gravitational potential energy between two radii is GMm(1/r1 - 1/r2). A body escapes a planet when its kinetic energy equals the potential energy needed to reach infinity, which gives the escape speed v = √(2GM/r).

Exam tip: use the zero of potential at infinity, and keep the sign of the potential negative in every calculation.

title: Abstract Data Types — Study Notes
content:
Abstract Data Types

What is an ADT?

An abstract data type is a logical description of a collection of data plus the operations on it, independent of implementation. Stacks, queues, linked lists, binary trees and hash tables are all ADTs; in A Level you must show how they are built from arrays or records with pointers.

Linked Lists

Each node holds a value and a pointer to the next node; a start pointer marks the head and a null marks the end. Insertion rewires two pointers — no shifting — giving O(1) insertion at a known position, but access requires walking the list, O(n).

Stacks and Queues

A stack is LIFO (push and pop at the top); a queue is FIFO (enqueue at the rear, dequeue from the front). Both can be arrays with index pointers or linked lists. Stack uses include call stacks and expression evaluation; queue uses include print buffers and breadth-first search.

Binary Search Trees

Each node has up to two children; left subtree keys are smaller, right subtree keys larger. Search, insert and (average-case) delete are O(log n). An in-order traversal outputs keys in ascending order. A degenerate (linear) tree from sorted input degrades to O(n).

Hash Tables

Covered in file organisation, but as an ADT a hash table pairs a hash function with bucket storage for O(1) average access.

Exam tips: be able to draw a tree after a sequence of insertions and write its three traversals; state the pointer changes for a linked-list insertion; compare ADT operations with Big-O.

title: Probability and Statistics II
content:
Probability and Statistics II

Normal Distribution

Continuous, bell-shaped, defined by mean μ and variance σ². Standardise: Z = (X − μ)/σ ~ N(0, 1).

Example: X ~ N(50, 4²). P(X > 56) = P(Z > 1.5) = 1 − 0.9332 = 0.0668.

Backwards problems: given a probability, find μ or σ from the z-value: x = μ + zσ.

Binomial Distribution

Fixed n independent trials, success probability p: P(X = r) = C(n, r) pʳ (1−p)^(n−r). Mean np, variance np(1 − p).

Example: n = 5, p = 0.2: P(X = 2) = 10 × 0.04 × 0.8³ = 0.2048.

Normal Approximation to Binomial

Valid when np > 5 and n(1 − p) > 5. Apply a continuity correction: P(X ≤ 10) becomes P(Y < 10.5) under Y ~ N(np, np(1−p)).

Expectation and Variance Rules

E(aX + b) = aE(X) + b; Var(aX + b) = a² Var(X). For sums: E(X + Y) = E(X) + E(Y).

Exam tips: always sketch the normal curve and shade the region; state the distribution you are using; never forget the continuity correction when approximating a discrete variable.

title: Exam technique: Scatter Diagrams
content:

For estimation questions, naming interpolation versus extrapolation earns a mark before any value, with the reliability comment credited separately.
### Traps
Error: claiming correlation proves causation. Correction: name the confounder (hot weather drives both). Error: trusting extrapolation like interpolation. Correction: outside the range is always less reliable. Error: forcing the line through the origin. Correction: anchor at (mean x, mean y). Error: calling curved association zero correlation. Correction: zero means no pattern at all.
### Worked example
A scatter diagram shows a positive correlation between hours revised and test score. The line of best fit passes through the mean point (x̄, ȳ). If x̄ = 5 and ȳ = 12 with gradient 2, the line is y = 2x + 2. Estimating y for x = 8 is interpolation if 8 lies within the data range, which makes it more reliable than extrapolating beyond the data.
### Check yourself
Explain why the line of best fit should pass through (x̄, ȳ). Check that 2 × 5 + 2 = 12, so the line does pass through the mean point. State whether a prediction at x = 20 would be interpolation or extrapolation, and say why it is less reliable.

title: Poisson Distribution — Study Notes
content:
The Poisson Distribution

The Model

X ~ Po(λ) counts events in a fixed interval of time or space when events occur independently, at a constant average rate λ, and never twice at the same instant. Classic settings: calls per hour at a helpdesk, typos per page, cars per minute at a quiet junction.

The Formula

P(X = r) = e^(−λ) λʳ / r! for r = 0, 1, 2, ...

Example: X ~ Po(2). P(X = 0) = e⁻² ≈ 0.1353. P(X = 1) = 2e⁻² ≈ 0.2707.

Mean and Variance

The defining signature of the Poisson:

  • E(X) = λ and Var(X) = λ — the mean and variance are equal.

If a question gives a mean m, then λ = m; the variance is also m.

Scaling the Interval

If X ~ Po(λ) per hour, then 3 hours gives Y ~ Po(3λ). Rates must be adjusted to the same interval before computing anything. Halving an interval halves λ.

Adding Poissons

If X ~ Po(λ₁) and Y ~ Po(λ₂) are independent, then X + Y ~ Po(λ₁ + λ₂). Two independent queues merging into one server produce a Poisson with summed rate.

Exam tips: check independence and constant rate before modelling — if events cluster (rush hours), Poisson fails. Convert the interval first: a rate of 8 per 20 minutes becomes 24 per hour. In "at least" questions use the complement exactly as with the binomial.

title: Algebra — Inequalities — Study Notes
content:
Algebra — Inequalities

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): solving linear inequalities, integer solution sets, shading regions on graphs (linear programming context).

1. Solving

Like equations, but reverse the sign when multiplying/dividing by a negative: −2x ≥ 6 ⇒ x ≤ −3.

Example: 3x − 5 < 2x + 1 ⇒ x < 6.

2. Integer solutions

−1 ≤ x < 4 ⇒ x ∈ {−1, 0, 1, 2, 3}. Closed endpoint for ≤/≥, open for </>.

3. Double inequalities

Handle both sides: −3 < 2x + 1 ≤ 7 → −4 < 2x ≤ 6 → −2 < x ≤ 3.

4. Shading regions

  • Draw the boundary line: dashed for </>, solid for ≤/≥.
  • Test a point (usually (0,0)) to pick the wanted side; shade the unwanted side or label the wanted region.
  • Feasible region satisfies all constraints simultaneously.

Example: y ≤ 2x + 1: solid line, test (0,0): 0 ≤ 1 ✓ → region containing origin.

Exam tips: never divide by an unknown sign — move x terms first; list integer solutions inside curly brackets; state which region you shade.

Solving linear inequalities

Inequalities are solved like equations, with one crucial exception: multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative number reverses the inequality sign. Answers are written as a single inequality such as x > 3, or as a set such as -2 < x ≤ 5 when two bounds are given.

Representing inequalities on a number line

An open circle marks a strict bound (< or >) that is not included; a filled circle marks an inclusive bound (≤ or ≥). Shade the region that satisfies the statement.

Regions on a coordinate grid

Draw each boundary line as a solid line for ≤ or ≥ and a dashed line for < or >. Test a point such as (0, 0) if it is not on the line; shade the side that makes the inequality true. Where several regions are required, the wanted region is the overlap of all the shaded areas. Integer points inside a region are counted when a question asks for them.

Worked example: solving a linear inequality

Solve 3x − 7 < 2x + 4. Subtract 2x from both sides to get x − 7 < 4, then add 7 to get x < 11. The solution set is every number less than 11, which has no lower bound.

Double inequalities and integer solutions

Solve −3 ≤ 2x + 1 < 7. Subtract 1 from each part: −4 ≤ 2x < 6. Divide each part by 2: −2 ≤ x < 3. The integer solutions are −2, −1, 0, 1 and 2. Remember that the ≤ sign includes −2 and the < sign excludes 3.

Multiplying or dividing by a negative number

Solve 8 − 3x > 2. Subtract 8: −3x > −6. Divide by −3 and reverse the sign: x < 2. Forgetting to reverse the sign is the most common lost mark in this topic.

Quadratic inequalities

Solve x² − x − 6 ≤ 0. Factorise to (x − 3)(x + 2) ≤ 0. The expression is zero at x = 3 and x = −2, and it is negative between them. The solution is −2 ≤ x ≤ 3. Sketch the parabola to see which region is below the axis.

Shading regions on a grid

  • Draw a boundary line as a solid line for ≤ or ≥, and as a dashed line for < or >.
  • Test a point that is not on the line, usually (0, 0) if the line does not pass through it, to decide which side to shade.
  • If the question asks for a region bounded by several inequalities, shade each one lightly and leave the overlap clear.

title: Functions — Study Notes
content:
Functions

A function maps each input in the domain to exactly one output in the range.

Composite Functions

fg(x) means f(g(x)) — apply g first, then f. Order matters.

Example: f(x) = 2x + 1, g(x) = x². Then fg(x) = 2x² + 1 but gf(x) = (2x + 1)².

Inverse Functions

f⁻¹ reverses f: f⁻¹f(x) = x. To find it, swap x and y in y = f(x) and rearrange.

Example: f(x) = 3x − 2 gives f⁻¹(x) = (x + 2)/3.

An inverse exists only if f is one-one. If not, restrict the domain (e.g. f(x) = x² for x ≥ 0 has f⁻¹(x) = √x). Graphically, y = f⁻¹(x) is the reflection of y = f(x) in the line y = x, and the range of f becomes the domain of f⁻¹.

Transformations

NotationEffect on y = f(x)
f(x) + atranslation up by a
f(x + a)translation left by a
a f(x)vertical stretch, factor a
f(ax)horizontal stretch, factor 1/a
−f(x)reflection in the x-axis
f(−x)reflection in the y-axis

Exam tips: state the domain of any inverse; when combining transformations, translations inside the bracket act in the opposite direction to the sign.

Composite and inverse functions: exam method

fg(x) means f(g(x)): apply g first, then f, so read the composite from the right. Check that the output of g lies in the domain of f before you combine them; restricted domains are a common examiner target.

To find f⁻¹(x), write y = f(x), swap x and y, then rearrange to make y the subject. The domain of f⁻¹ is the range of f. A function has an inverse only if it is one-to-one on the domain given; restrict the domain (for example x ≥ 0 for a quadratic) when the question asks for it.

The graph of f⁻¹ is the reflection of the graph of f in the line y = x, so the point (a, b) on f becomes (b, a) on f⁻¹. Use this to check an answer.

Exam cue: State the domain and range of an inverse when asked, and write fg and gf separately when order matters.

title: Exam technique: Web Technologies and Security
content:
### What earns the marks
For trust, the CA signature chain described earns both marks: CA binds key to identity, browsers check against roots. For bulk data, symmetric speed plus asymmetric key exchange earns the hybrid pair. For verification, re-hash and compare stated earns the integrity mark with mismatch meaning change.
### Traps
Error: encryption claimed to stop phishing. Correction: valid TLS carries fake sites too; check identity. Error: hashes claimed to prove authorship. Correction: hashes prove integrity, signatures prove authorship. Error: self-claims accepted as trust. Correction: only CA signatures establish it.

title: Quadratics — Study Notes
content:
Quadratics

A quadratic has the form ax² + bx + c with a ≠ 0. Master three tools: completing the square, the discriminant, and inequalities.

Completing the Square

Rewrite x² + bx + c as (x + b/2)² − (b/2)² + c.

Example: x² + 6x + 5 = (x + 3)² − 9 + 5 = (x + 3)² − 4, so the vertex is at (−3, −4).

For a > 1, factor out a first: 2x² + 12x + 19 = 2(x² + 6x) + 19 = 2(x + 3)² − 18 + 19 = 2(x + 3)² + 1.

Vertex form a(x − h)² + k gives the minimum/maximum value k at x = h — this is how you find a maximum area or minimum cost.

The Discriminant

Δ = b² − 4ac decides how the curve meets the x-axis:

ΔRootsGraph
Δ > 0two distinct real rootscrosses x-axis twice
Δ = 0repeated roottouches (tangent)
Δ < 0no real rootsnever meets x-axis

Example: kx² + 4x + 1 = 0 has equal roots when 16 − 4k = 0, so k = 4.

Quadratic Inequalities

Solve by sketching. For x² − 5x + 4 < 0, factorise: (x − 1)(x − 4) < 0, and the curve is below the axis between the roots, so 1 < x < 4.

Tip: flip the inequality when dividing by a negative number, and always sketch to check which interval you need.

Curve and Line Intersections

Set the equations equal; the resulting quadratic's discriminant tells you if the line is a secant (Δ > 0), tangent (Δ = 0) or misses (Δ < 0).

Exam tips: complete the square before reading off turning points; state the discriminant condition explicitly before solving for an unknown coefficient.

title: Dynamics — Study Notes
content:
Dynamics

Newton's Laws

  • A body stays at rest or in uniform motion unless acted on by a resultant force.
  • F = ma — the resultant force equals mass × acceleration.
  • Forces occur in pairs: equal magnitude, opposite direction, on different bodies.

Example: a 2 kg mass with a 10 N resultant accelerates at 5 m s⁻².

Weight and Mass

Weight W = mg — a force in newtons; mass in kg is invariant. A 70 kg person weighs about 687 N.

Momentum

p = mv (vector, kg m s⁻¹). Resultant force = rate of change of momentum: F = Δp/Δt.

Conservation: in a collision with no external forces, total momentum is unchanged.

  • Elastic: kinetic energy also conserved
  • Inelastic: some KE becomes heat/sound

Example: a 3 kg trolley at 4 m s⁻¹ hits a stationary 1 kg trolley and they couple: 12 = 4v, so v = 3 m s⁻¹.

Friction and Connected Bodies

Draw free-body diagrams, then apply F = ma along each axis. For a towed car and trailer, the tow-bar tension appears as an internal pair (equal and opposite).

Exam tips: 'constant velocity' means zero resultant force, not zero friction; impulse questions want FΔt = Δp.

title: Trigonometry — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Trigonometry

Mathematics — AS (9709). Use the symmetry of the graphs. For sin x = 1/2 in 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π: the acute answer is π/6, and the second solution is π − π/6 = 5π/6.

Key areas to revise

  • Exact Values
  • Key Identities
  • Solving Equations
  • Graphs and Transformations
  • Using Identities

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Worked example

Solve 2 sin x = −1 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 360°. Rearrange to sin x = −1/2. The reference angle is 30°, and sine is negative in the third and fourth quadrants, so x = 180° + 30° = 210° and x = 360° − 30° = 330°. Both answers go in the final line, because a question that asks for "all solutions in the interval" loses marks when one is missing.

Common mistakes

  • Stopping at the calculator value and missing the second solution in the interval.
  • Giving answers in degrees when the question asks for radians, or the reverse. Check the units against the question before writing the final answer.
  • Dividing both sides of an equation by a trig expression that could be zero, which loses solutions. Factorise and set each factor to zero instead.

title: Poisson Distribution — Study Notes
content:
The Poisson Distribution

The Model

X ~ Po(λ) counts events in a fixed interval of time or space when events occur independently, at a constant average rate λ, and never twice at the same instant. Classic settings: calls per hour at a helpdesk, typos per page, cars per minute at a quiet junction.

The Formula

P(X = r) = e^(−λ) λʳ / r! for r = 0, 1, 2, ...

Example: X ~ Po(2). P(X = 0) = e⁻² ≈ 0.1353. P(X = 1) = 2e⁻² ≈ 0.2707.

Mean and Variance

The defining signature of the Poisson:

  • E(X) = λ and Var(X) = λ — the mean and variance are equal.

If a question gives a mean m, then λ = m; the variance is also m.

Scaling the Interval

If X ~ Po(λ) per hour, then 3 hours gives Y ~ Po(3λ). Rates must be adjusted to the same interval before computing anything. Halving an interval halves λ.

Adding Poissons

If X ~ Po(λ₁) and Y ~ Po(λ₂) are independent, then X + Y ~ Po(λ₁ + λ₂). Two independent queues merging into one server produce a Poisson with summed rate.

Exam tips: check independence and constant rate before modelling — if events cluster (rush hours), Poisson fails. Convert the interval first: a rate of 8 per 20 minutes becomes 24 per hour. In "at least" questions use the complement exactly as with the binomial.

Exam method: Poisson probabilities

If X ~ Po(λ), then P(X = r) = e^(−λ) λʳ / r! for r = 0, 1, 2, … The mean and the variance are both equal to λ, so the parameter is found directly from either quantity given in the question.

Use the calculator's Poisson function or the formula with the exact value of e^(−λ). When a question asks for P(X ≤ r) or P(X ≥ r), add the separate probabilities, or subtract the complement from 1.

The rate must match the interval. If events occur at 4 per hour and the question asks about a 30-minute period, the new mean is 2. Always rescale λ to the period in the question.

A Poisson model is appropriate for counts of events that occur randomly and independently at a constant average rate.

Exam cue: Check the rescaling of λ first; it is the most common error in Poisson questions, and it costs the whole question.

title: Thermal Physics — Study Notes
content:
Thermal Physics

Internal Energy

Sum of random kinetic + potential energies of molecules. Temperature rise → KE up; phase change → PE up (bonds stretch) at constant temperature.

Specific Heat and Latent Heat

  • Heating: Q = mcΔθ (c = specific heat capacity)
  • Phase change: Q = mL (L = specific latent heat)

Example: melting 0.2 kg ice: Q = 0.2 × 334,000 ≈ 67 kJ — no temperature change during the change.

Mixtures: heat lost = heat gained.

Gas Laws

  • Boyle: pV = constant (T fixed)
  • Charles: V/T = constant (p fixed)
  • Pressure law: p/T = constant (V fixed)
  • Combined/ideal: pV = nRT, R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹

Example: 2 mol at 300 K in 0.05 m³: p = nRT/V = 2 × 8.31 × 300/0.05 ≈ 100 kPa.

Kinetic Theory

½m⟨c²⟩ = (3/2)kT — temperature measures mean translational KE. Also pV = ⅓Nm⟨c²⟩.

Exam tips: use kelvin in every gas equation; in mixture problems, work per substance with a common final temperature.

title: Algebra — Graphs — Study Notes
content:
Algebra — Graphs

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): straight lines (gradient, intercept), key curves (quadratic, cubic, reciprocal, exponential), tangents, kinematic reading.

1. Straight lines

  • Gradient m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁).
  • y = mx + c; parallel ⇒ equal m; perpendicular ⇒ m₁m₂ = −1.

Example: through (2, −1) parallel to y = 3x + 1: y + 1 = 3(x − 2) ⇒ y = 3x − 7.

2. Drawing curves

Table of values, plot, smooth curve. Parabola symmetry axis x = −b/2a. Recognise reciprocal y = 1/x (two branches) and exponential y = aˣ (through (0,1)).

3. Interpreting

  • Roots = x-intercepts; y-intercept from x = 0.
  • Turning points of quadratics by completing the square.

4. Tangents and rates

Gradient of tangent at a point = instantaneous rate: draw a large triangle, rise/run. Area under a speed–time graph = distance (trapezium estimate).

5. Graphical solutions

Simultaneous: intersection points. Quadratic = line: intersections give roots. Read off carefully to the accuracy allowed.

Exam tips: quote gradients as fractions where exact; when estimating a tangent gradient, use a triangle spanning at least 4 grid squares.

title: Nuclear Physics — Study Notes
content:
Nuclear Physics

The nucleus

The nucleus holds protons and neutrons, collectively nucleons. Nuclide notation ᴬZX gives Z protons and A nucleons, so N = A − Z neutrons. Isotopes share Z and differ in N. Nuclear densities are about 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³, so nearly all the mass of an atom sits in a tiny volume.

Mass defect and binding energy (23.1)

The mass of a nucleus is less than the sum of the masses of its separate nucleons. This difference is the mass defect Δm. Energy equivalent to Δm, given by E = Δmc², is the binding energy: the energy released when the nucleus is assembled from separate nucleons, and the energy needed to separate it. In nuclear work, 1 u = 931 MeV.

Example: a mass defect of 0.0300 u corresponds to E = 0.0300 × 931 ≈ 27.9 MeV.

The binding energy per nucleon peaks near iron-56, the most tightly bound nucleus. Energy is released when the nucleons move toward this peak, by fission of heavy nuclei or by fusion of light ones.

Radioactive decay (23.2)

Decay is random and spontaneous. The effect of each type on the nucleus and its penetration are:

TypeWhat changesStopped by
alphaZ − 2, A − 4paper
beta-minusZ + 1, A unchangeda few mm of aluminium
gammano change to Z or Athick lead

The activity A = λN is the rate of decay, in becquerel (Bq). The decay constant λ and the half-life t½ are related by λ = ln 2 / t½. The number of nuclei left after time t is N = N₀e^(−λt).

Example: a sample with t½ = 10 days has 1/8 of its original activity after 30 days, since three half-lives have passed.

Example: with t½ = 5.0 h = 1.8 × 10⁴ s, λ = 0.693 / 1.8 × 10⁴ ≈ 3.9 × 10⁻⁵ s⁻¹.

Fission and fusion

Heavy nuclei split (fission) into lighter nuclei of greater binding energy per nucleon, which releases energy in reactors. Light nuclei merge (fusion), which releases energy in stars.

Exam tips: balance Z and A on both sides of every decay equation. Convert the half-life to seconds before finding λ. Use A = λN, not guesswork with halves, when the number of nuclei is needed.

title: Exam technique: Sets
content:
### What earns the marks
For Venn problems, the union formula n(A union B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A intersect B) quoted earns the method mark; subtracting the intersection corrects the double count explicitly. For neither, the subtraction from the universal set shown earns the final mark. For notation, the complement symbol with the correct parent set earns precision marks.
### Traps
Error: adding all three Venn counts including the intersection. Correction: the overlap was counted twice, subtract once. Error: element confused with subset (2 vs {2}). Correction: only a set can be a subset. Error: empty set equated with {0}. Correction: {0} has one element; the empty set has none. Error: modal-style single numbers for grouped answers. Correction: classes are intervals.

title: Pressure & Density — Study Notes
content:
Pressure & Density

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): pressure & pressure differences in fluids, density review (Extended pressure-depth).

1. Pressure basics

p = F/A (Pa = N/m²). Increase F or decrease A to raise pressure; explain applications (snowshoes, knives, hydraulic press).

2. Liquids

  • Pressure increases with depth: p = ρgh (Extended).
  • Same level, same liquid ⇒ same pressure (hydrostatic paradox).
  • Hydraulic systems transmit pressure — force multiplier: F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂.

3. Atmospheric pressure

~10⁵ Pa at sea level; demonstrated by collapsing can, mercury barometer 760 mmHg; decreases with altitude.

4. Density revisited

ρ = m/V; floating condition; upthrust = weight of displaced fluid (qualitative).

5. Gas pressure (particle model)

Particles collide with walls → force per area. Volume ↓ at same T ⇒ pressure ↑ (more frequent collisions). Temperature ↑ ⇒ faster particles ⇒ more frequent, harder impacts.

title: Algebra — Simplifying and Expanding — Study Notes
content:
Algebra — Simplifying and Expanding

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): substitution, collecting like terms, expanding brackets, factorising (common factor, quadratics, difference of two squares), algebraic fractions.

1. Substitution

a = 3, b = −2: 2a² − b = 2(9) + 2 = 20. Always bracket substituted negatives.

2. Collecting like terms

5x + 3y − 2x + y = 3x + 4y. Terms need identical letter parts (x² and x are not like terms).

3. Expanding

  • Single: 3(2x − 5) = 6x − 15.
  • Double: (x + 3)(x − 4) = x² − x − 12 (grid or FOIL).
  • Cubic products: (x+2)³ = x³ + 6x² + 12x + 8.

4. Factorising

  • Common factor: 6x²y − 9xy² = 3xy(2x − 3y).
  • Quadratics: x² − 5x + 6 = (x − 2)(x − 3) (two numbers ×6, sum −5).
  • Harder: 6x² + 7x + 2 = (3x + 2)(2x + 1) — split the middle term.
  • Difference of two squares: 9x² − 25 = (3x − 5)(3x + 5).

5. Algebraic fractions

Factorise top and bottom fully, then cancel: (x² − 9)/(x + 3) = (x − 3). To add, use a common denominator: 1/(x+1) + 2/(x−1) = (3x + 1)/((x+1)(x−1)).

Exam tips: always factorise out the highest common factor including the number; check expansion by substituting x = 1 into both forms.

title: Data Representation — Study Notes
content:
Data Representation

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): binary/hex, two's complement, BCD, text/image/sound encoding, file sizes, compression.

1. Number systems

  • Binary place values 128…1; hex digits 0–9, A–F; one hex digit = one nibble (4 bits).
  • Conversions: binary ↔ decimal ↔ hex. 0101 1010 → 5A; FF = 255.
  • BCD: 4 bits per decimal digit — 0029 → 0000 0000 0010 1001. Used in clocks/calculators; easier digit conversions, more bits than pure binary.

2. Two's complement (signed)

MSB is negative: −128 64 32 16 8 4 2 1. −5 = 1111 1011. Range 8-bit: −128…+127.

Negating: invert bits, add 1. Subtraction: add the negated number — 7 − 5 = 7 + (−5) = 0000 0111 + 1111 1011 = 0000 0010.

3. Text

ASCII 7-bit (128 chars) → extended sets; Unicode for all scripts (UTF-8 variable width). Character sets map codes to glyphs; uppercase/lowercase codes differ by one bit.

4. Images and sound

  • Bitmap: pixels; colour depth = bits per pixel. File size (bits) = W × H × depth. Metadata (width, height, depth) stores dimensions.
  • Sound: sample rate (Hz), resolution (bits per sample), track duration × channels. Higher rate/depth = better fidelity, larger files.

5. Compression

  • Lossless (RLE, ZIP): exact restore — text/code must use it. RLE example: AAABBBCC → 3A3B2C; effective with runs.
  • Lossy (JPEG, MP3): discards perceptually minor data — photos/music OK, text never.

Exam tips: show full working in conversions; for size questions write the formula first with units; state the reason a compression type suits the file.

Binary addition and overflow

Binary addition follows the same carry rule as denary, except that 1 + 1 = 10 (0 carry 1). For example, 0110 + 0111 = 1101. A register or storage location has a fixed number of bits, so a result that needs more bits than are available overflows and gives a wrong answer. Programmers and examiners look for an overflow error when the carry out of the leftmost bit is set.

Exam tip: state the number of bits used. Overflow depends on that width, not on the value of the numbers alone.

title: Exam technique: Measures of Variation
content:
### What earns the marks
For standard deviation, mean first then the squared-deviation sum earns each mark. For coded data, the y-bar and s_y transformation earns the method mark. For comparisons, mean and spread commented together earns both marks.
### Traps
Error: variance reported as sd. Correction: root last. Error: comparing means only. Correction: comment on spread too. Error: coding applied once then forgotten. Correction: transform consistently.
### Worked example
Five values are 2, 4, 4, 6 and 9. The mean is 25 / 5 = 5. The squared deviations are 9, 1, 1, 1 and 16, which sum to 28. The variance is 28 / 5 = 5.6, and the standard deviation is the square root, about 2.37. Show the squared deviations line on the paper, since the method mark depends on it.
### Check yourself
If each value in the list is increased by 10, state what happens to the mean and to the standard deviation. The mean rises by 10, while the standard deviation is unchanged, because adding a constant does not change the spread.

### Worked example
Five values are 2, 4, 4, 6 and 9. The mean is 25 / 5 = 5. The squared deviations are 9, 1, 1, 1 and 16, which sum to 28. The variance is 28 / 5 = 5.6, and the standard deviation is the square root, about 2.37. Show the squared deviations line on the paper, since the method mark depends on it.
