title: Quadratics — Study Notes
content:
Quadratics

A quadratic has the form ax² + bx + c with a ≠ 0. Master three tools: completing the square, the discriminant, and inequalities.

Completing the Square

Rewrite x² + bx + c as (x + b/2)² − (b/2)² + c.

Example: x² + 6x + 5 = (x + 3)² − 9 + 5 = (x + 3)² − 4, so the vertex is at (−3, −4).

For a > 1, factor out a first: 2x² + 12x + 19 = 2(x² + 6x) + 19 = 2(x + 3)² − 18 + 19 = 2(x + 3)² + 1.

Vertex form a(x − h)² + k gives the minimum/maximum value k at x = h — this is how you find a maximum area or minimum cost.

The Discriminant

Δ = b² − 4ac decides how the curve meets the x-axis:

ΔRootsGraph
Δ > 0two distinct real rootscrosses x-axis twice
Δ = 0repeated roottouches (tangent)
Δ < 0no real rootsnever meets x-axis

Example: kx² + 4x + 1 = 0 has equal roots when 16 − 4k = 0, so k = 4.

Quadratic Inequalities

Solve by sketching. For x² − 5x + 4 < 0, factorise: (x − 1)(x − 4) < 0, and the curve is below the axis between the roots, so 1 < x < 4.

Tip: flip the inequality when dividing by a negative number, and always sketch to check which interval you need.

Curve and Line Intersections

Set the equations equal; the resulting quadratic's discriminant tells you if the line is a secant (Δ > 0), tangent (Δ = 0) or misses (Δ < 0).

Exam tips: complete the square before reading off turning points; state the discriminant condition explicitly before solving for an unknown coefficient.

Discriminant and inequalities: exam method

For ax² + bx + c = 0 the discriminant is b² − 4ac. Positive gives two distinct real roots, zero gives one repeated root, and negative gives no real roots. Use this without solving the equation when the question asks about the nature of the roots.

To find the values of k for which a quadratic has no real roots, require b² − 4ac < 0 and solve the resulting inequality in k.

To solve a quadratic inequality, find the roots, sketch the U-shaped (a > 0) or inverted-U (a < 0) curve, and read off the region above or below the axis. For x² − 5x + 6 < 0 the roots are 2 and 3, and the solution is 2 < x < 3.

Exam cue: Completing the square gives the turning point (p, q) and shows the minimum or maximum value directly.

title: Geometry — Congruence and Similarity — Study Notes
content:
Geometry — Congruence and Similarity

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): congruence criteria, similar shapes, scale factors for length/area/volume, symmetry.

1. Congruence

Criteria: SSS, SAS, ASA (AAS), RHS. State the criterion used when proving triangles congruent, then transfer matching sides/angles.

2. Similarity

Equal angles + sides in proportion. Scale factor k = corresponding new ÷ old.

Example: triangles with sides 4, 6, 8 and 6, 9, 12: k = 1.5.

3. Length, area, volume factors

Length ×k; area ×k²; volume ×k³ — including reverse problems.

Example: volumes 250 cm³ and 2000 cm³: k³ = 8 ⇒ k = 2 ⇒ areas ×4.

4. Area/volume calculations from similarity

Find k from a matching length pair, then apply the right power. Watch hidden pairs (radii, heights, slants).

5. Symmetry

Line symmetry (reflect) and rotational symmetry order — for 2-D shapes and 3-D solids (prisms, cubes, pyramids).

Exam tips: write the matching-vertex order in similarity statements (△ABC ~ △DEF); choose which k-power applies before calculating.

Congruent triangles

Two triangles are congruent when they match on one of four conditions: SSS (three sides), SAS (two sides and the included angle), ASA or AAS (two angles and a side), or RHS (right angle, hypotenuse and a side) for right-angled triangles. SSA is not a condition. Name the congruence test in every proof.

Similar shapes and scale factors

Similar shapes have equal angles and proportional sides. The linear scale factor k multiplies lengths, k² multiplies areas and k³ multiplies volumes. To find a missing side, set up the ratio of corresponding sides and cross-multiply.

Transformations in geometry questions

A translation is described by a column vector, a rotation by its centre, angle and direction, a reflection by its mirror line and an enlargement by its centre and scale factor. Image points are checked by measuring the same distance from the centre or the mirror line.

title: Exam technique: Continuous Random Variables
content:
### What earns the marks
For pdf constants, total area equals 1 stated earns the method mark. For probabilities, the integral with correct limits earns each mark. For mean and variance, E(X) and E(X squared) - E(X) squared each earn credit stepwise.
### Traps
Error: point probabilities given positive values. Correction: points have zero area. Error: mean mistaken for median. Correction: solve the half-area equation for medians. Error: variance sign reversed. Correction: E(X squared) minus mean squared.
### Worked example
A pdf is f(x) = kx for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2. Total area is 1, so the integral of kx from 0 to 2 gives 2k = 1 and k = 1/2. Then P(X > 1) is the integral of x/2 from 1 to 2, which is [x²/4] from 1 to 2 = 1 − 1/4 = 3/4. The mean is the integral of x · x/2 from 0 to 2, which is 8/6 = 4/3.
### Check yourself
For the same pdf, state why P(X = 1) is zero before you calculate anything. A single point has zero width, so its area is zero.

### Worked example
A pdf is f(x) = kx for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2. Total area is 1, so the integral of kx from 0 to 2 gives 2k = 1 and k = 1/2. Then P(X > 1) is the integral of x/2 from 1 to 2, which is [x²/4] from 1 to 2 = 1 − 1/4 = 3/4. The mean is the integral of x · x/2 from 0 to 2, which is 8/6 = 4/3.
### Check yourself
For the same pdf, state why P(X = 1) is zero before you calculate anything. A single point has zero width, so its area is zero.

title: Energy, Work & Power — Study Notes
content:
Energy, Work & Power

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2023–2025): stores and transfers, KE/PE, work, energy sources, power, efficiency.

1. Energy stores & transfers

Stores: kinetic, gravitational, elastic, chemical, nuclear, thermal. Transfer mechanisms: mechanically, electrically, heating, waves. Energy is conserved overall; transfers via work done.

2. Formulas

  • KE = ½mv²; PE = mgh.
  • Work W = Fd (force along displacement, joules).
  • Power P = W/t = E/t; P = Fv for constant speed.

Example: 0.5 kg at 4 m/s: KE = 4 J. Lift 2 kg by 3 m: PE = 60 J (g = 10).

3. Energy sources

Renewable: solar, wind, hydro, geothermal, biofuel, tidal — replenished. Non-renewable: fossil fuels, nuclear — finite. Discuss reliability, cost, pollution for "evaluate" questions.

4. Efficiency

Efficiency = useful output ÷ total input (×100%). Sankey diagrams show losses.

Example: motor: 150 J useful from 600 J → 25%.

5. Energy-chain problems

Equating KE loss to PE gain: v = √(2gh) for frictionless drop; braking distance grows with v².

Exam tips: define work as "force × distance moved in the direction of the force"; use g = 10 unless told otherwise; efficiency is a ratio — no units.

title: Binomial Distribution — Study Notes
content:
The Binomial Distribution

When Binomial Applies

X ~ B(n, p) counts successes in n independent trials when:

  • a fixed number n of identical trials,
  • each trial ends in success or failure,
  • constant success probability p,
  • trials are independent.

Check all four before using the model — "justifying a binomial model" is a real exam question.

The Formula

P(X = r) = ⁿCᵣ pʳ(1 − p)ⁿ⁻ʳ for r = 0, 1, ..., n. The ⁿCᵣ counts which r of the n trials were the successes.

Example: X ~ B(5, 0.3). P(X = 2) = ¹⁰C₂? No — ⁵C₂ × 0.3² × 0.7³ = 10 × 0.09 × 0.343 = 0.3087.

Cumulative Probabilities

P(X ≤ 2) = P(0) + P(1) + P(2). "At least" questions convert by the complement: P(X ≥ 2) = 1 − P(X ≤ 1). Keep one extra decimal place in intermediate steps to avoid rounding drift.

Expectation and Variance

  • E(X) = np and Var(X) = np(1 − p)

For X ~ B(20, 0.4): E(X) = 8 and Var(X) = 4.8.

Modelling Decisions

If trials are dependent (drawing without replacement from a small population) binomial is not appropriate. If p changes between trials it is not binomial. When n is large and p small, the binomial is approximately Poisson — but at A2 you usually stay exact.

Exam tips: identify n and p in words before touching the calculator. For P(X ≥ k) always rewrite as 1 − P(X ≤ k − 1). Tables give cumulative values — use them rather than summing by hand.

Exam method: binomial probabilities

If X ~ B(n, p) then X counts successes in n independent trials, each with probability p. P(X = r) = nCr p^r (1 - p)^(n - r) for r = 0, 1, ..., n. The mean is np and the variance is np(1 - p).

Check the conditions first: a fixed number of trials, two outcomes, a constant p and independent trials. If any condition fails, the binomial model does not apply.

Exam cue: Always state n and p before calculating, and say which condition you are checking. For P(X ≥ r) or P(X > r), use the complement 1 − P(X ≤ r − 1), read from the cumulative table or calculator, and state the final probability to three significant figures.

Design Approaches

  • Top-down (stepwise refinement): decompose into modules — planned structure
  • Object-oriented: classes encapsulating state + behaviour — reusability

Pseudocode Conventions

DECLARE x : INTEGER
IF x > 10 THEN ... ELSE ... ENDIF
WHILE ... ENDWHILE
FOR i ← 1 TO n ... NEXT i
FUNCTION f(a) RETURNS INTEGER

Searching

  • Linear: check each item, O(n), works unsorted
  • Binary: halve a sorted list each step, O(log n)

Example: 1,000,000 items: binary search needs ≤ 20 comparisons.

Sorting

AlgorithmBestAverageIdea
BubbleO(n)O(n²)swap neighbours
InsertionO(n)O(n²)insert into sorted prefix
MergeO(n log n)O(n log n)divide and merge

Merge sort example: [5,2,9,1] → [5,2][9,1] → [2,5][1,9] → [1,2,5,9].

Recursion

A function calling itself with a base case. Factorial: f(0)=1, f(n)=n·f(n−1). Stack frames handle state.

Ethics, Security & Impact

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): ethics & professional codes, security threats, malware, online safety, environmental/employment impact.

1. Ethics and codes

ACM/IEEE-CS/BCS codes: public interest, competence, integrity, privacy. Applying: identify the principle → apply to scenario → stakeholders affected → consequences.

2. Threats

  • Malware: virus (attaches, replicates via host), worm (self-spreads), trojan (disguised), spyware, ransomware.
  • Social: phishing (fake emails/sites), pharming (DNS/hosts redirect), shoulder surfing, brute force.
  • Technical: interception (packet sniffing), SQL injection (malicious input into queries), DoS (flooding services).

3. Defences

Antivirus/antispyware (scan, quarantine), firewalls (port/IP filtering), 2FA + biometrics, strong passwords + managers, encryption (HTTPS, VPN), access levels, patches/updates, user training.

4. Online behaviour

Digital footprint, cyberbullying, fake news, privacy settings, verification of sources.

5. Wider impact

Employment: automation displaces roles but creates IT jobs. Environment: e-waste, energy use vs paperless efficiency. Monitoring: workplace tracking, CCTV — balance with privacy laws (GDPR-style).

Exam tips: name the threat precisely (pharming ≠ phishing), then the matched defence; ethics answers need principle + application, not opinion.

Number — Sets

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): set notation, Venn diagrams, shading, universal set, subsets.

1. Notation

  • ∈ belongs to; ∉ not in; ∅ empty set; ξ (or U) universal set; n(A) = number of elements.
  • A ∩ B intersection (AND); A ∪ B union (OR); A′ complement (NOT A).
  • A ⊆ B: every element of A is in B.

2. Venn diagrams

Fill the intersection first, then work outwards. Two sets: only A, both, only B, neither.

Example: 30 students; 18 maths, 15 physics, 7 both ⇒ neither = 30 − (11 + 7 + 8) = 4.

3. Shading

For A ∩ B′ shade where A and outside-B overlap. (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′ (De Morgan) — check every region.

4. Regions algebra

With region variables x, y, z: use the totals to form equations, e.g. n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B).

5. Probability links

P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B) — inclusion–exclusion from the diagram.

Exam tips: "neither" sits outside both circles — subtract from the universal set last; label regions with numbers, not expressions, as you fill.

title: Kinematics — Study Notes
content:
Kinematics

Definitions

  • Distance and speed are scalars; displacement s and velocity v are vectors (magnitude and direction).
  • Velocity v = ds/dt: rate of change of displacement.
  • Acceleration a = dv/dt: rate of change of velocity. A change of direction at constant speed is still an acceleration.

Graphs

  • Gradient of a displacement–time graph = velocity. A horizontal line means the object is at rest.
  • Gradient of a velocity–time graph = acceleration. A straight line with constant gradient means uniform acceleration.
  • Area under a velocity–time graph = displacement. Area below the time axis counts as negative (a return journey).
  • Area under an acceleration–time graph = change in velocity.

SUVAT equations (uniform acceleration only)

EquationQuantity not involved
v = u + ats
s = ut + ½at²v
v² = u² + 2ast
s = ½(u + v)ta

Choose the equation that leaves out the quantity you were not given or do not need. Sign convention matters: take up (or the direction of motion) as positive. For objects falling freely, take g = −9.81 m s⁻² if up is positive.

Non-uniform motion

  • When acceleration is not constant, SUVAT cannot be used. Work from the graphs instead.
  • Average speed = total distance ÷ total time. Average velocity = total displacement ÷ total time. These are not the same when the object changes direction.
  • Read the gradient at a point on a curved s–t or v–t graph from the tangent at that point.

Projectiles

Resolve the launch velocity into independent components. Horizontal: uₓ = u cos θ, constant velocity, s = uₓt. Vertical: u_y = u sin θ, uniform acceleration g downwards, so SUVAT applies. At the highest point v_y = 0. For a launch and landing at the same level, time of flight = 2u_y/g.

Worked example: a ball is launched at 20 m s⁻¹ at 30° above the horizontal. uₓ = 20 cos 30° ≈ 17.3 m s⁻¹ and u_y = 20 sin 30° = 10 m s⁻¹. Time of flight = 2 × 10 / 9.81 ≈ 2.04 s. Range = 17.3 × 2.04 ≈ 35 m.

Exam tips: write the sign convention at the top of the answer. Treat the horizontal and vertical motions as two separate one-dimensional problems linked only by time. Check whether the question asks for speed or velocity, and distance or displacement.

title: Coordinate Geometry — Study Notes
content:
Coordinate Geometry

Gradients and Equations of Lines

Gradient m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁). From ax + by + c = 0, the gradient is −a/b.

Point-slope form: y − y₁ = m(x − x₁).

Example: through (4, 3) with m = −1/2: y − 3 = −(x − 4)/2, i.e. y = −x/2 + 5.

Parallel and Perpendicular

  • Parallel lines: equal gradients.
  • Perpendicular lines: m₁m₂ = −1 (gradients are negative reciprocals).

Example: perpendicular to y = 2x + 1 has gradient −1/2.

Midpoint and Distance

Midpoint of (x₁, y₁), (x₂, y₂): ((x₁+x₂)/2, (y₁+y₂)/2).

Distance: √((x₂−x₁)² + (y₂−y₁)²). The line from (0,0) to (3,4) has length 5 — recognise 3-4-5 triangles.

Intersections and Bisectors

Intersections: solve the equations simultaneously. The perpendicular bisector of AB passes through the midpoint of AB with gradient −1/m(AB) — equate distances PA = PB for the locus method.

Exam tips: rationalise gradients as fractions; check perpendicularity by multiplying gradients to get −1.

title: Exam technique: Dynamics
content:
### What earns the marks
For resultant force, subtract opposition before applying F = ma to earn both marks. For collisions, total momentum before equated to total after earns the method mark. For rebounds, the sign change included earns the second mark.
### Traps
Error: friction ignored in acceleration. Correction: use the resultant, not the push alone. Error: rebound treated as stopping. Correction: add the speeds with the sign flip. Error: kinetic energy claimed conserved generally. Correction: momentum always, kinetic only when elastic.
### Worked example
A car of mass 800 kg has a driving force of 2400 N and a resistance of 400 N. The resultant force is 2400 - 400 = 2000 N, so a = F/m = 2000 / 800 = 2.5 m/s^2. Subtract the opposing force before you divide by the mass.
### Check yourself
A 2 kg trolley moving at 3 m/s hits a stationary 1 kg trolley, and they stick together. Total momentum before is 2 x 3 = 6 kg m/s, so the joint speed is 6 / 3 = 2 m/s. Show the momentum equation even when the speed looks obvious.

title: Exam technique: Sequences and Series
content:
### What earns the marks
For AP terms, a + (n-1)d with the brackets evaluated earns the mark; sums use n/2(2a + (n-1)d) quoted. For GP work, the ratio found by division earns one mark and the formula applied earns the next. For sum to infinity, the |r| < 1 check stated earns the method mark.
### Traps
Error: n used instead of (n-1) in terms. Correction: first term needs zero gaps. Error: infinity sums with |r| >= 1. Correction: check convergence first. Error: differentiating S_n for the nth term. Correction: subtract S_{n-1}.
### Worked example
An arithmetic progression has a = 5 and d = 3. The 20th term is a + 19d = 5 + 57 = 62. The sum of the first 20 terms is S₂₀ = (20/2)(2a + 19d) = 10 × 67 = 670. A geometric progression with terms 2, 6, 18 has r = 3, so S₅ = 2(3⁵ − 1)/(3 − 1) = 242. The sum to infinity exists only when |r| < 1, so for r = 1/2 with a = 8 the sum is 8 / (1 − 1/2) = 16.
### Check yourself
State the nth term of a sequence from its sum. Find Sₙ, then subtract Sₙ₋₁. Do not differentiate Sₙ, because the sum is a discrete function.

### Worked example
An arithmetic progression has a = 5 and d = 3. The 20th term is a + 19d = 5 + 57 = 62. The sum of the first 20 terms is S₂₀ = (20/2)(2a + 19d) = 10 × 67 = 670. A geometric progression with terms 2, 6, 18 has r = 3, so S₅ = 2(3⁵ − 1)/(3 − 1) = 242. The sum to infinity exists only when |r| < 1, so for r = 1/2 with a = 8 the sum is 8 / (1 − 1/2) = 16.

title: Operating Systems — Study Notes
content:
Operating Systems

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): OS roles, memory/process management, hardware–software layer, interrupts, buffers, utility software.

1. What an OS does

Manages memory, processes/files, I/O via drivers, security (users, permissions), and provides the UI (CLI/GUI) between user, applications and hardware.

2. Memory and process management

  • Paging/segmentation move programs in/out; virtual memory extends RAM to disk when RAM is full.
  • Multitasking: scheduler gives each process time slices; context switching saves/restores state.

3. Interrupts and buffers

Interrupts signal events (I/O complete, timer); CPU saves context, services via ISR, resumes. Buffers hold data in transit (printing) so slow devices don't block the CPU; spooling queues jobs.

4. Utility software

Disk formatter, defragmenter (reduces head movement on HDDs; unnecessary for SSD), backup scheduler, compression, antivirus, file compression.

5. UI and drivers

CLI: precise, scriptable, low overhead. GUI: icons/windows, discoverable, more resources. Device drivers translate OS calls to hardware specifics — each device needs its own.

Exam tips: "manage" verbs earn marks: manages memory, manages processes, manages peripherals; explain virtual memory by RAM-full scenario, not definition alone.

Interrupts and scheduling

An interrupt is a signal that tells the processor to stop its current task and deal with an event, such as a key press, a timer ending or an error. The processor saves the state of the current task, runs the interrupt service routine, and then resumes the task it was doing. Interrupts let the processor respond to devices without checking them constantly.

The operating system manages several programs at once through scheduling. Each program receives processor time in turn, which gives the impression that they run at the same time. Memory management keeps each program's data separate, and the operating system provides a user interface and manages files and devices.

Exam tip: describe the steps of an interrupt in order: save state, run the routine, restore state.

title: Motion in a Circle and Gravity — Study Notes
content:
Motion in a Circle and Gravity

Circular Motion

Angular speed ω = v/r = 2π/T (rad s⁻¹). Centripetal acceleration a = v²/r = ω²r, always directed to the centre; centripetal force F = mv²/r.

Example: a 0.5 kg ball on a 1 m string at 2 m s⁻¹ needs F = 2 N inward.

Gravitational Field

Newton's law: F = Gm₁m₂/r², G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².

Field strength g = GM/r². At Earth's surface g ≈ 9.81 N kg⁻¹.

Orbits

For a circular orbit, gravity supplies the centripetal force: GMm/r² = mv²/r, so v = √(GM/r) — higher orbits move slower but have longer periods (Kepler's third law: T² ∝ r³).

Geostationary satellites: T = 24 h, r ≈ 42,300 km from the centre.

Potential

Gravitational potential φ = −GM/r (zero at infinity). Potential gradient gives field strength: g = −dφ/dr.

Exam tips: speed in orbit is independent of the satellite's own mass; don't confuse g at the surface with orbital equations using r from the planet's centre.

title: Exam technique: Probability
content:
### What earns the marks

Correction: condition first, population second. Error: adding P(A) + P(B) without subtracting the overlap. Correction: both-occurring counted twice. Error: adding single-coin probabilities for two coins. Correction: multiply along branches.

A bag holds 3 red and 2 blue counters. Two are drawn without replacement. P(both red) = 3/5 × 2/4 = 3/10. Write each branch fraction with its changed denominator before multiplying. P(at least one red) is quicker as 1 − P(both blue) = 1 − (2/5 × 1/4) = 9/10.

title: Data Representation — Study Notes
content:
Data Representation

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): binary/hex, two's complement, BCD, text/image/sound encoding, file sizes, compression.

1. Number systems

  • Binary place values 128…1; hex digits 0–9, A–F; one hex digit = one nibble (4 bits).
  • Conversions: binary ↔ decimal ↔ hex. 0101 1010 → 5A; FF = 255.
  • BCD: 4 bits per decimal digit — 0029 → 0000 0000 0010 1001. Used in clocks/calculators; easier digit conversions, more bits than pure binary.

2. Two's complement (signed)

MSB is negative: −128 64 32 16 8 4 2 1. −5 = 1111 1011. Range 8-bit: −128…+127.

Negating: invert bits, add 1. Subtraction: add the negated number — 7 − 5 = 7 + (−5) = 0000 0111 + 1111 1011 = 0000 0010.

3. Text

ASCII 7-bit (128 chars) → extended sets; Unicode for all scripts (UTF-8 variable width). Character sets map codes to glyphs; uppercase/lowercase codes differ by one bit.

4. Images and sound

  • Bitmap: pixels; colour depth = bits per pixel. File size (bits) = W × H × depth. Metadata (width, height, depth) stores dimensions.
  • Sound: sample rate (Hz), resolution (bits per sample), track duration × channels. Higher rate/depth = better fidelity, larger files.

5. Compression

  • Lossless (RLE, ZIP): exact restore — text/code must use it. RLE example: AAABBBCC → 3A3B2C; effective with runs.
  • Lossy (JPEG, MP3): discards perceptually minor data — photos/music OK, text never.

Exam tips: show full working in conversions; for size questions write the formula first with units; state the reason a compression type suits the file.

title: Scatter Diagrams and Correlation — Study Notes
content:
Scatter Diagrams and Correlation

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): scatter diagrams, types of correlation, line of best fit, interpolation vs extrapolation.

1. Correlation types

  • Positive: both increase (revision time vs score).
  • Negative: one increases, other decreases (price vs demand).
  • No correlation: random scatter.
  • Strength: strong (tight to a line) vs weak (loose).

2. Line of best fit

Balance points either side of the line; it need not pass through the origin. Use two well-separated points on your line (not necessarily data points) to estimate its gradient and equation.

Example: line through (10, 24) and (50, 60): m = 36/40 = 0.9 → y = 0.9x + 15.

3. Using the line

Interpolation (inside the data range) is reliable; extrapolation (outside) is a risk — say so if asked.

4. Correlation ≠ causation

A third factor may drive both variables (ice-cream sales and drownings both rise with temperature). Describe relationships, don't over-claim.

5. Outliers

Points far from the trend: identify, and comment on their effect on the line; ignore them when drawing the best fit if instructed.

Exam tips: describe correlation in full ("strong positive linear correlation"); quote the equation only from two points on the drawn line, not raw data.

title: Algebra — Sequences and Functions — Study Notes
content:
Algebra — Sequences and Functions

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): nth term (linear & quadratic), special sequences, function notation, composites, inverses.

1. Linear sequences

nth term = a + (n − 1)d. 5, 8, 11, … → 3n + 2. Check n = 1, 2, 3.

2. Quadratic sequences

Second difference = 2a → an² + bn + c. 3, 8, 15, 24 … has second difference 2 → n² + bn + c; subtract n² → 2, 4, 6, 8 → 2n; so nth term = n² + 2n.

3. Special sequences

Even/odd, triangular (½n(n+1)), squares, cubes, Fibonacci-type (each term = sum of previous two), geometric (×r).

4. Function notation

f(x) = 2x − 5: f(3) = 1. Solve f(x) = 11 → x = 8.

5. Composite functions

fg(x) = f(g(x)) — g first. f(x) = 2x − 5, g(x) = x²: gf(2) = g(1) = 1; fg(3) = f(9) = 13.

6. Inverse functions

Swap x and y, rearrange. f(x) = 2x − 5 ⇒ f⁻¹(x) = (x + 5)/2. Domain of inverse = range of original. Verify: f⁻¹(f(x)) = x.

Exam tips: write the bracket order explicitly in composites; show the "swap and rearrange" line for inverses — answer-only scores little.

title: Information Representation — Study Notes
content:
`# Information Representation

Number Systems and Ranges

Unsigned binary with n bits stores 0 to 2ⁿ − 1. Two's complement represents negatives: the MSB has value −2ⁿ⁻¹.

Example: 8-bit two's complement of −5: 11111011 (−128 + 64 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 2 + 1).

SystemBaseDigits
Binary20–1
Hexadecimal160–9, A–F
BCD—4 bits per decimal digit

Binary Arithmetic

Add: 0+0=0, 0+1=1, 1+1=0 carry 1, 1+1+1=1 carry 1. Overflow happens when a result exceeds the word size.

Subtraction uses two's complement addition (A − B = A + (−B)).

Text

  • ASCII: 7 bits, 128 characters, English only
  • Unicode: universal scripts; UTF-8 is variable-width (1–4 bytes)

Images and Sound

  • Bitmap: pixels with colour depth (bits per pixel). File size = width × height × depth.
  • Sound: sampling rate (Hz) × bit depth × duration × channels.
  • Resolution trade-off: fidelity vs size.

Compression

  • Lossless (ZIP, run-length encoding): exact reconstruction — required for text/code
  • Lossy (JPEG, MP3): discards perceptually minor data — smaller files

Example: RLE of AAABBBCC → 3A3B2C.

Exam tips: show working for two's complement conversions; state why compression type suits the data (text must be lossless).

Binary and hexadecimal worked conversion

To convert the denary number 156 to binary, subtract the place values from the largest downwards: 156 = 128 + 16 + 8 + 4, so the binary value is 10011100. Each binary digit is a bit, and the place values double from right to left: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128.

Hexadecimal groups four bits at a time, so one hexadecimal digit represents a value from 0 to 15. Split 10011100 into 1001 and 1100 to get 9 and 12, which is 9C in hexadecimal. Hexadecimal is used to write memory addresses and colour codes because it is shorter than binary and converts to it directly.

Exam tip: show the place-value working, not just the answer. Examiners award method marks for the subtraction or the grouping.

title: Thermal Physics — Study Notes
content:
Thermal Physics

Temperature and scales

Thermodynamic temperature is measured in kelvin. The kelvin and Celsius scales have the same size of degree, with T/K = θ/°C + 273. Absolute zero (0 K) is the lowest possible temperature, at which the particles of an ideal gas have minimum kinetic energy.

Example: 25 °C = 298 K.

Specific heat capacity and latent heat

Specific heat capacity c is the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 K: Q = mcΔθ. Latent heat is the energy needed to change the state of 1 kg without a change in temperature: Q = mL. Melting and boiling absorb energy without a temperature rise, because the energy goes into breaking intermolecular bonds, not into kinetic energy.

Example: warming 2.0 kg of water (c = 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) by 10 K needs 84 kJ. Melting 0.20 kg of ice (L = 334 kJ kg⁻¹) needs 67 kJ.

The mole and Avogadro constant

One mole contains N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ particles. The number of particles is N = nN_A, where n is the amount in moles. Molar mass is the mass of one mole, in kg mol⁻¹ in SI units.

Equation of state for an ideal gas

pV = nRT, where R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and T must be absolute. Equivalently pV = NkT, with k = R/N_A = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹.

Example: 0.10 mol at 300 K in 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³ has p = nRT/V ≈ 1.2 × 10⁵ Pa.

Kinetic theory

The pressure of an ideal gas comes from molecules colliding with the container walls. The mean kinetic energy of a molecule is ⟨Ek⟩ = 3kT/2, so it depends only on the absolute temperature. At 300 K it is about 6.2 × 10⁻²¹ J.

Internal energy and the first law

The internal energy of an ideal gas is the sum of the kinetic and potential energies of its molecules. For an ideal gas there are no intermolecular forces, so internal energy depends only on temperature. The first law of thermodynamics is ΔU = Q + W, where Q is heat added to the system and W is work done on the system. Heat lost by a system is therefore negative.

Example: a gas has 500 J of work done on it and loses 200 J of heat. ΔU = −200 + 500 = +300 J.

Exam tips: convert to kelvin before using pV = nRT or the kinetic-energy formula. Check the sign convention for W in the question. Use latent heat only when the temperature is constant.

title: Magnetism & Electromagnetism — Study Notes
content:
Magnetism & Electromagnetism

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2023–2025): magnets & fields; magnetic effect of a current; force on a current-carrying conductor; motor effect; electromagnetic induction (Extended); transformers (Extended).

1. Magnets and fields

Iron/steel/cobalt/nickel; like poles repel. Field lines exit N, enter S; compass plotting; plotting compass aligns with field. Induced magnetism: iron (temporary) vs steel (permanent).

2. Electromagnets

Solenoid field like a bar magnet; strength ↑ with current, turns, iron core. Uses: relays, scrapyard crane, electric bell, speaker. Hard/soft magnetic materials choose permanent vs core use.

3. Force on a current-carrying conductor

F = BIL, direction by Fleming's left hand (fIeld, current, force). Reversing current or field reverses force. D.C. motor: coil, commutator reverses current each half-turn for continuous rotation; speed/torque ↑ with current, field strength, turns/area.

4. Electromagnetic induction (Extended)

Induced e.m.f. when a conductor cuts field lines or flux changes. Fleming's right hand (generator). Factors: speed, field strength, turns. A.C. generator: slip rings; dynamo effect; Lenz's law opposes change (direction of induced current).

5. Transformers (Extended)

Vp/Vs = Np/Ns; Pin ≈ Pout (100% assumed): IpVp = IsVs. Step-up raises V, lowers I → lower I²R transmission losses; a.c. required (changing flux).

title: Exam technique: Information Representation
content:
### What earns the marks
For two complement, inversion plus one stated earns the method mark before the value. For floating point, mantissa plus exponent roles stated earn one mark each. For normalisation, the leading-bit rule quoted earns the precision mark.
### Traps
Error: sign bit ignored in range. Correction: an n-bit signed range tops at 2^(n-1) - 1. Error: larger exponent read as more precision. Correction: exponent sets range, mantissa sets precision. Error: normalised form guessed. Correction: mantissa starts with 0.1 or 1.0 pattern per the scheme.
### Worked example
Write -45 in 8-bit two's complement. First write 45 in binary: 00101101. Invert every bit to get 11010010, then add 1 to get 11010011. Check: the sign bit has weight -128, so the value is -128 + 64 + 16 + 2 + 1 = -45, which matches.
### Check yourself
State the range of an 8-bit two's complement integer, and say which bit sets the sign. The range is -128 to +127, and the leftmost bit is the sign bit with weight -128.

title: Exam technique: Communication and Networking
content:
### What earns the marks
For switching and protocols, describe earns marks for the mechanism plus its consequence: packets carry addresses and sequence numbers so routers forward independently and the receiver reassembles. For TCP vs UDP, justify earns marks for matching reliability to the use case, not for declaring one better. For security, name earns the control plus what it inspects: packet-filtering checks headers against rules.
### Traps
Error: circuit-switching features credited to packet switching. Correction: dedicated path and guaranteed bandwidth are circuit properties. Error: TCP recommended for live video. Correction: delay hurts more than loss there, so UDP. Error: claiming wireless uses collision detection. Correction: senders cannot listen while sending, so avoidance (RTS/CTS).
### Worked example
A local area network of computers in one room connects to the internet through a router. The router uses the IP address to send packets to the correct network. Each computer's network card has a MAC address that is fixed at manufacture, and a switch uses it to deliver frames within the local network.
### Check yourself
Explain the difference between an IP address and a MAC address. An IP address is logical and can change, for example when a device joins another network. A MAC address is physical and identifies the network card itself.

title: Oscillations and Waves II — Study Notes
content:
Oscillations and Waves II

Progressive vs Stationary

Progressive waves transfer energy; stationary waves store it in loops. Stationary patterns arise from two identical waves travelling in opposite directions (reflections on strings, air columns).

PropertyProgressiveStationary
Amplitudesame for all pointsvaries: nodes zero, antinodes max
Phasevaries along wavesame within a loop, π flip across nodes
Energytransferredtrapped

Harmonics

A string fixed at both ends: f₁ = v/2L, then 2f₁, 3f₁… Closed pipes resonate at odd multiples; open pipes at all multiples.

Superposition Applications

  • Young's double slit: x = λD/a — evidence light is a wave
  • Diffraction grating: d sin θ = nλ — resolution of spectra
  • Noise-cancelling headphones: destructive interference of antiphase sound

Polarization Applications

Polaroid sunglasses cut glare from horizontal surfaces; stress analysis in plastics; LCD screens control light with twisted polarizers. Malus' law I = I₀cos²θ.

Exam tips: 'explain' marks want the physics: path difference, phase, node/antinode conditions — not just formula substitution.

title: Work, Energy and Power — Study Notes
content:
Work, energy and power

Work

  • Work done = force × displacement in the direction of the force, W = Fs cos θ. Unit: joule (J), where 1 J = 1 N m.
  • No work is done by a force that acts perpendicular to the displacement, such as the normal contact force on a body moving along a horizontal surface.

Energy stores and transfers

Gravitational potential energy, kinetic energy, elastic potential energy, chemical energy and thermal energy are energy stores. Work done transfers energy from one store to another.

Conservation of energy

Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred. Where only conservative forces such as gravity act, the total mechanical energy is constant. Where non-conservative forces such as friction or air resistance act, the energy they dissipate appears as thermal energy.

Kinetic and gravitational potential energy

  • Kinetic energy: Ek = ½mv².
  • Gravitational potential energy change near the Earth's surface: ΔEp = mgΔh.

Power and efficiency

  • Power = work done ÷ time = energy transferred ÷ time. Unit: watt (W), where 1 W = 1 J s⁻¹.
  • Efficiency = useful energy output ÷ total energy input × 100%. It is always less than 100%.

Worked example: a 2.0 kg object falls freely from rest through 5.0 m. Its speed at the bottom, from energy conservation: ½mv² = mgh, so v = √(2gh) = √(2 × 9.81 × 5.0) ≈ 9.9 m s⁻¹.

Exam tips: check whether the question says air resistance is negligible before using conservation of energy. Always convert minutes to seconds in power calculations. Give efficiency as a percentage.

title: Nuclear Physics — Study Notes
content:
Nuclear Physics

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): nuclear model, radioactivity, decay types, half-life, safety, fission/fusion (Extended).

1. The nuclear model

Nucleus (protons +, neutrons 0) with orbiting electrons (−). Nuclide notation ᴬ_Z X. Isotopes: same Z, different A. Rutherford scattering established the nuclear model; proton number Z, nucleon number A.

2. Radiation types

TypeNatureRange (air)Stopped by
alpha αhelium nucleus (2p2n)few cmpaper
beta β⁻fast electron~20–30 cmfew mm aluminium
gamma γEM wavevery farthick lead/concrete

Deflection in fields: α/β opposite, γ none. Ionising: α > β > γ. Background radiation: radon, cosmic, rocks, medical, fallout.

3. Decay equations

  • α: A −4, Z −2 (e.g. ²³⁸₉₂U → ²³⁴₉₀Th + α).
  • β⁻: neutron → proton; A same, Z +1 (e.g. ¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₇N + β⁻).
  • γ: no change to A or Z.

Balance A and Z on both sides — that is the check.

4. Half-life

Time for half the unstable nuclei to decay (random process). Read from a decay curve or count halves: 80 → 40 → 20 over two half-lives.

Example: 800 Bq, half-life 2 h → 200 Bq after 4 h.

5. Safety and uses

Uses: medical tracers (β/γ), sterilisation, thickness gauge (β), dating (C-14), smoke alarms (α). Safety: distance, time, shielding, wear badges, store in lead. Handle with tongs; never point at people.

6. Fission and fusion (Extended)

Fission: heavy nucleus splits (U-235 + neutron), chain reaction controlled by moderators/control rods — power stations. Fusion: light nuclei join (stellar) — needs huge T/P; releases more energy per kg; no long-lived waste.

Nuclear decay and half-life

Alpha particles are helium nuclei with two protons and two neutrons, and they are strongly ionising but have low penetration. Beta-minus emission happens when a neutron changes into a proton and an electron is emitted. Gamma radiation is electromagnetic, carries no charge and no mass, and has high penetration. Background radiation must be subtracted from measured count rates before a half-life is calculated.

title: Exam technique: Probability (A2)
content:
### What earns the marks
For conditional probability, the restricted sample space stated earns the method mark. For independence checks, P(A)P(B) compared with P(A and B) earns both marks. For Bayes-style updates, the tree fractions multiplied along branches earn stepwise credit.
### Traps
Error: mutually exclusive assumed independent. Correction: test, never assume. Error: given-condition ignored. Correction: shrink the denominator first. Error: branches added instead of multiplied. Correction: multiply along, add across.
### Worked example
Event A has P(A) = 0.5 and event B has P(B) = 0.4. Given that A and B are independent, P(A and B) = 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.20. If the question instead gives P(A and B) = 0.3, then the events are not independent, because 0.3 does not equal 0.20. The conditional probability is P(A | B) = P(A and B) ÷ P(B) = 0.3 ÷ 0.4 = 0.75.
### Check yourself
Two events are mutually exclusive with P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.2. Are they independent? No. P(A and B) = 0 but P(A)P(B) = 0.06, so the events are dependent. Mutually exclusive events are always dependent when both have non-zero probability.
